title: Be Verb (am / is / are)
subtitle: The most fundamental verb — to be
keyPoint: The verb "be" changes to am / is / are depending on the subject. For negatives, just add "not" after it.

useCases.label: Profession
useCases.example: I am a teacher.
useCases.translation: I am a teacher.

useCases.label: State / Feeling
useCases.example: She is tired.
useCases.translation: She is tired.

useCases.label: Location
useCases.example: We are at home.
useCases.translation: We are at home.

examples.en: I am 25 years old.
He is a doctor.
They are not here.
Is she your sister?

mistakes.wrong: I is happy.
mistakes.right: I am happy.
mistakes.note: After I, always use am.

mistakes.wrong: He are a student.
mistakes.right: He is a student.
mistakes.note: After He/She/It, use is.

mistakes.wrong: They is from Korea.
mistakes.right: They are from Korea.
mistakes.note: After They, use are.

quiz.question: She ___ my best friend.
quiz.explanation: She is 3rd person singular, so use is.

quiz.question: We ___ students.
quiz.explanation: We is plural, so use are.

quiz.question: I ___ not tired.
quiz.explanation: After I, always use am.

quiz.question: Which sentence is correct?
quiz.explanation: They + are is the correct combination.

tip: You can contract am/is/are: I'm, she's, they're. These contractions sound much more natural in conversation!

title: Present Simple
subtitle: Habits, routines and facts
keyPoint: Use this for habits, routines and permanent facts. Add -s to the verb when He/She/It is the subject.

useCases.label: Habits & Routines
useCases.example: I drink coffee every morning.
useCases.translation: I drink coffee every morning.

useCases.label: Facts & Truths
useCases.example: The sun rises in the east.
useCases.translation: The sun rises in the east.

useCases.label: Likes & Preferences
useCases.example: She loves music.
useCases.translation: She loves music.

examples.en: I wake up at 7am every day.
He plays football on weekends.
We don't eat meat.
Does she live in Seoul?

mistakes.wrong: She work in a hospital.
mistakes.right: She works in a hospital.
mistakes.note: He/She/It + verb always takes -s/-es.

mistakes.wrong: He don't like spicy food.
mistakes.right: He doesn't like spicy food.
mistakes.note: 3rd person singular negatives use doesn't.

mistakes.wrong: Does she likes pizza?
mistakes.right: Does she like pizza?
mistakes.note: After Does, use the base verb. No -s needed.

quiz.question: She ___ to work by bus.
quiz.explanation: She is 3rd person singular, so use goes.

quiz.question: They ___ not drink alcohol.
quiz.explanation: They is plural, so use do not (don't).

quiz.question: ___ he speak French?
quiz.explanation: 3rd person singular questions use Does.

quiz.question: Water ___ at 100°C.
quiz.explanation: Scientific facts use present simple. It (water) → boils.

tip: 3rd person singular rule: verbs ending in -s/-sh/-ch/-x/-o add -es. Examples: watches, goes, fixes

title: Articles: a / an / the
subtitle: Small words, big difference
keyPoint: Use a/an for first mention, the for something already known. Use an before vowel sounds.

useCases.label: First mention (a/an)
useCases.example: I bought a new phone.
useCases.translation: I bought a new phone.

useCases.label: Second mention (the)
useCases.example: The phone is great.
useCases.translation: The phone is great.

useCases.label: Unique in the world (the)
useCases.example: The sun is bright today.
useCases.translation: The sun is bright today.

examples.en: I have a cat and a dog.
examples.ko: 저는 고양이와 개를 한 마리씩 키우고 있어요.

examples.en: The cat is black.
She is an engineer.
I love the moon.

mistakes.wrong: I am a engineer.
mistakes.right: I am an engineer.
mistakes.note: Before a vowel sound (e), use an.

mistakes.wrong: The life is short.
mistakes.right: Life is short.
mistakes.note: No article needed for abstract concepts in general.

mistakes.wrong: I go to the school.
mistakes.right: I go to school.
mistakes.note: School, hospital etc. are used without the when referring to their purpose.

quiz.question: She is ___ doctor.
quiz.explanation: doctor starts with a consonant (d), so use a.

quiz.question: ___ Earth is round.
quiz.explanation: Earth is unique in the world, so use The.

quiz.question: I ate ___ orange.
quiz.explanation: orange starts with a vowel (o), so use an.

quiz.question: ___ love is beautiful.
quiz.explanation: No article needed when talking about abstract concepts in general.

tip: Use an before silent h too: an honest man, an hour. The rule is about sound, not spelling!

title: Basic Questions
subtitle: Yes/No and Wh- questions
keyPoint: For Yes/No questions, move the verb to the front. Wh- questions start with a question word.

useCases.label: Yes/No Questions
useCases.example: Is he your brother?
useCases.translation: Is he your brother?

useCases.label: Asking for info
useCases.example: What is your name?
useCases.translation: What is your name?

useCases.label: Asking about place
useCases.example: Where do you work?
useCases.translation: Where do you work?

examples.en: Are you from Japan?
What do you do?
Where does he live?
Who is your favourite singer?

mistakes.wrong: Where you live?
mistakes.right: Where do you live?
mistakes.note: Even after a question word, you still need do/does.

mistakes.wrong: What she likes?
mistakes.right: What does she like?
mistakes.note: Use does for third-person singular.

mistakes.wrong: Do you are a student?
mistakes.right: Are you a student?
mistakes.note: Don't use do/does in questions with be verbs.

quiz.question: ___ you like coffee?
quiz.explanation: For ordinary verbs with you, use Do.

quiz.question: Where ___ she work?
quiz.explanation: She is 3rd person singular, so use does.

quiz.question: ___ your name?
quiz.explanation: What's = What is. This is the most natural form.

quiz.question: Who ___ your English teacher?
quiz.explanation: The structure is Who + be verb + subject.

title: Past Simple
subtitle: Talking about completed past events
keyPoint: Regular verbs add -ed; irregular verbs must be memorised. Use did for negatives and questions.

useCases.label: Completed past action
useCases.example: I finished work at 6pm.
useCases.translation: Work finished at 6pm.

useCases.label: Historical facts
useCases.example: He was born in 1990.
useCases.translation: He was born in 1990.

useCases.label: Sequence of events
useCases.example: I woke up, ate, and left.
useCases.translation: I woke up, ate and left.

examples.en: I visited my grandmother yesterday.
She didn't eat breakfast this morning.
Did you watch the game last night?
They went to the beach last summer.

mistakes.wrong: I didn't went there.
mistakes.right: I didn't go there.
mistakes.note: After didn't, use the base verb form. went → go

mistakes.wrong: Did she came?
mistakes.right: Did she come?
mistakes.note: After Did, use the base verb.

mistakes.wrong: I have went yesterday.
mistakes.right: I went yesterday.
mistakes.note: Use past simple, not present perfect, with specific past time expressions like yesterday.

quiz.question: She ___ a movie last night.
quiz.explanation: last night is a past time expression, so use the past tense watched.

quiz.question: They ___ not go to school.
quiz.explanation: Past negatives use didn't (= did not).

quiz.question: ___ you enjoy the concert?
quiz.explanation: Past questions start with Did.

quiz.question: Which past tense form is correct?
quiz.explanation: came is the correct irregular past form of come.

tip: Key irregular verbs to memorise: go→went, have→had, see→saw, come→came, give→gave, take→took, make→made

title: Present Continuous
subtitle: Actions happening right now
keyPoint: Use be + verb-ing to describe actions happening right now.

useCases.label: Right now
useCases.example: I am writing an email.
useCases.translation: I am writing an email right now.

useCases.label: Temporary situation
useCases.example: She is staying at a hotel.
useCases.translation: She is staying at a hotel.

useCases.label: Near future plans
useCases.example: We are meeting tomorrow.
useCases.translation: We are meeting tomorrow.

examples.en: The children are playing outside.
I am not feeling well today.
Is it raining outside?
She is learning Korean these days.

mistakes.wrong: I am knowing the answer.
mistakes.right: I know the answer.
mistakes.note: State verbs like know, like, want, love are not used in the continuous form.

mistakes.wrong: She is eat dinner.
mistakes.right: She is eating dinner.
mistakes.note: In continuous tenses, always add -ing to the verb.

mistakes.wrong: They are work hard.
mistakes.right: They are working hard.
mistakes.note: After the be verb, use the -ing form, not the base verb.

quiz.question: He ___ a book right now.
quiz.explanation: Right now signals something happening at this moment — use continuous.

quiz.question: I ___ (not) feel hungry.
quiz.explanation: The negative of I + am is am not.

quiz.question: ___ they ___ the game?
quiz.explanation: Are + they + watching — correct continuous question structure.

quiz.question: Which verb CANNOT be used in the continuous tense?
quiz.explanation: Believe is a state verb and cannot be used in continuous tenses.

tip: Present simple vs continuous: "I eat rice" (every day) vs "I am eating rice" (right now)

title: Comparatives & Superlatives
subtitle: Comparing things and people
keyPoint: Use -er/more to compare two things; use -est/most for the extreme among three or more.

useCases.label: Comparing two (than)
useCases.example: Seoul is bigger than Busan.
useCases.translation: Seoul is bigger than Busan.

useCases.label: Superlative (3 or more)
useCases.example: She is the tallest in the class.
useCases.translation: She is the tallest in the class.

useCases.label: Equal comparison (as~as)
useCases.example: He is as tall as his father.
useCases.translation: He is as tall as his father.

examples.en: This coffee is hotter than that one.
It's the most expensive restaurant here.
Today is better than yesterday.
She runs faster than anyone else.

mistakes.wrong: She is more tall than me.
mistakes.right: She is taller than me.
mistakes.note: 1-2 syllable adjectives take -er. No need for more.

mistakes.wrong: He is the most fast runner.
mistakes.right: He is the fastest runner.
mistakes.note: Short adjectives like fast take -est.

mistakes.wrong: This is more good.
mistakes.right: This is better.
mistakes.note: The comparative of good is better (irregular).

quiz.question: Mount Everest is ___ mountain in the world.
quiz.explanation: When comparing within a group of more (the world), use the superlative: the highest.

quiz.question: My bag is ___ than yours.
quiz.explanation: 2-syllable adjectives ending in -y change to -ier: heavy → heavier.

quiz.question: English is ___ French for me.
quiz.explanation: Use comparative + than. easy → easier.

quiz.question: Which superlative form is correct?
quiz.explanation: Short vowel + single consonant: double the consonant — big → biggest.

tip: Some 2-syllable adjectives can take -er/-est: simple→simpler, clever→cleverer. Both forms are acceptable!

title: Present Perfect
subtitle: Connecting past actions to the present
keyPoint: Use have/has + past participle for past experiences, recent results and ongoing situations.

useCases.label: Experience (ever/never)
useCases.example: Have you ever tried sushi?
useCases.translation: Have you ever tried sushi?

useCases.label: Result (just/already)
useCases.example: I have just finished work.
useCases.translation: I have just finished work.

useCases.label: Duration (for/since)
useCases.example: She has lived here since 2010.
useCases.translation: She has lived here since 2010.

examples.en: I have never eaten octopus.
She has already left the office.
We have known each other for 10 years.
Have you seen this film yet?

mistakes.wrong: I have went to Paris.
mistakes.right: I have been to Paris.
mistakes.note: have been to = experience of visiting. went is a simple past verb.

mistakes.wrong: She has finished it yesterday.
mistakes.right: She finished it yesterday.
mistakes.note: With specific past times like yesterday, use the past simple, not present perfect.

mistakes.wrong: Have you ever went?
mistakes.right: Have you ever been?
mistakes.note: Use Have + past participle (been). went is a simple past form.

quiz.question: I ___ never ___ to Australia.
quiz.explanation: have + been (present perfect for experience).

quiz.question: She ___ already ___ dinner.
quiz.explanation: She is 3rd person singular → has. Past participle: eaten.

quiz.question: How long ___ you ___ here?
quiz.explanation: Duration + present perfect: have lived.

quiz.question: Which sentence correctly uses present perfect?
options: She has seen that film last week.
He has ate breakfast an hour ago.
quiz.explanation: just is a key time expression for present perfect.

tip: for = duration (for 3 years), since = starting point (since 2020). Both are used with present perfect!

title: Modal Verbs
subtitle: Ability, obligation, possibility and permission
keyPoint: Modal verbs are always followed by the base verb. can=ability, must=obligation, should=advice, might=possibility.

cells: I can swim. Can I help?

useCases.label: Ability (can)
useCases.example: She can speak five languages.
useCases.translation: She speaks five languages.

useCases.label: Obligation (must)
useCases.example: You must not smoke here.
useCases.translation: You must not smoke here.

useCases.label: Advice (should)
useCases.example: You should drink more water.
useCases.translation: You should drink more water.

useCases.label: Possibility (might)
useCases.example: He might be at home.
useCases.translation: He might be at home.

examples.en: You should apologise to her.
It might snow tomorrow.
Can you help me with this?
You must not park here.

mistakes.wrong: She can to swim.
mistakes.right: She can swim.
mistakes.note: After modal verbs, use the base verb — no to.

mistakes.wrong: You should to rest.
mistakes.right: You should rest.
mistakes.note: After should, use the base verb — no to.

mistakes.wrong: He musts go now.
mistakes.right: He must go now.
mistakes.note: Modal verbs never change form, even with third-person singular.

quiz.question: You ___ drink and drive. It's illegal.
quiz.explanation: For prohibition, use must not (= mustn't).

quiz.question: ___ you pass me the salt, please?
quiz.explanation: Could is used for polite requests.

quiz.question: She ___ be tired. She worked 12 hours.
quiz.explanation: might = possibility (not certain, but it could happen).

quiz.question: You ___ see a dentist soon.
quiz.explanation: should = advice and recommendation.

tip: must vs have to: both show obligation but must = personal decision, have to = external rule. "I must study" vs "I have to study (school rule)"

title: Passive Voice
subtitle: Focusing on the action, not the actor
keyPoint: The passive is formed with be + past participle. Add the agent with "by" if needed.

useCases.label: Unknown / unimportant agent
useCases.example: My wallet was stolen.
useCases.translation: My wallet was stolen.

useCases.label: Formal / news style
useCases.example: The law was passed.
useCases.translation: The law was passed.

useCases.label: Scientific / academic
useCases.example: Water is made of H₂O.
useCases.translation: Water is made of H₂O.

examples.en: The Eiffel Tower was built in 1889.
Spanish is spoken in 20 countries.
The email has been sent.
The cake was eaten by the children.

mistakes.wrong: The book is write by her.
mistakes.right: The book is written by her.
mistakes.note: Passive voice = be + past participle. write → written.

mistakes.wrong: It was builded in 1900.
mistakes.right: It was built in 1900.
mistakes.note: The past participle of build is built (irregular).

mistakes.wrong: The work is did by him.
mistakes.right: The work is done by him.
mistakes.note: The past participle of do is done.

quiz.question: The letter ___ yesterday.
quiz.explanation: yesterday = past. Passive past = was sent.

quiz.question: The Pyramids ___ by the Egyptians.
quiz.explanation: Past fact, passive voice: were built.

quiz.question: English ___ all over the world.
quiz.explanation: General present fact, passive present: is spoken.

quiz.question: Change to passive: "Someone broke the window."
quiz.explanation: Active past (broke) → Passive past: was broken.

tip: When in doubt, use the active voice! The passive is most natural when the agent is unknown or unimportant.

title: First Conditional
subtitle: Real and possible future conditions
keyPoint: Use for real and possible future situations. If + present simple, will + base verb.

cells: I'll stay home if it rains.

useCases.label: Possible condition
useCases.example: If I pass the exam, I will celebrate.
useCases.translation: If I pass, I will celebrate.

useCases.label: Warning / threat
useCases.example: If you touch that, it will break.
useCases.translation: If you touch that, it will break.

useCases.label: Promise / offer
useCases.example: If you help me, I'll buy you lunch.
useCases.translation: If you help me, I will buy you lunch.

examples.en: If you study hard, you will pass.
She will be late if she doesn't hurry.
If it snows, we won't go out.
examples.ko: 눈이 오면 우리는 나가지 않을 거예요.

examples.en: What will you do if you lose your job?

mistakes.wrong: If it will rain, I will stay.
mistakes.right: If it rains, I will stay.
mistakes.note: Do not use will in the if-clause. Use present tense.

mistakes.wrong: If she will come, we start.
mistakes.right: If she comes, we will start.
mistakes.note: if-clause = present tense; result clause = will + base verb.

mistakes.wrong: If I am tired, I will sleep.
mistakes.right: If I feel tired, I will sleep.
mistakes.note: A concrete verb is more natural than a state expression here.

quiz.question: If you ___ hard, you ___ succeed.
quiz.explanation: 1st conditional: if + present (work), result = will succeed.

quiz.question: I'll call you if I ___ the answer.
quiz.explanation: Use present tense (know) in the if-clause.

quiz.question: If it ___ sunny, we ___ to the beach.
quiz.explanation: if-clause = is (present), result clause = will go.

quiz.question: Which sentence is a correct first conditional?
options: If she will come, I am happy.
If it rains, I stay home.
If you eat this, you will feel better.
If he studied, he will pass.
quiz.explanation: if-clause present (eat) + result will + verb (feel). Correct 1st conditional.

tip: Unless = If not: "Unless you hurry, you will be late" = "If you don't hurry, you will be late"

title: Second Conditional
subtitle: Imaginary situations, different from reality
keyPoint: Use for imaginary situations opposite to current reality. If + past simple, would + base verb.

cells: If I had a million dollars...
If I were (formal) / If I was (informal)

useCases.label: Unreal / imaginary
useCases.example: If I could fly, I would go to Paris.
useCases.translation: If I could fly, I would go to Paris.

useCases.label: Giving advice
useCases.example: If I were you, I would apologise.
useCases.translation: If I were you, I would apologise.

useCases.label: Dreams & wishes
useCases.example: If I lived by the sea, I would swim every day.
useCases.translation: If I lived by the sea, I would swim every day.

examples.en: If I won the lottery, I would buy a house.
What would you do if you lost your phone?
If I were a bird, I would fly to the sea.
She would help if she could.
examples.ko: 그녀는 할 수 있다면 도와줄 거예요.

mistakes.wrong: If I would have money, I would travel.
mistakes.right: If I had money, I would travel.
mistakes.note: Do not use would in the if-clause. Use past tense (had).

mistakes.wrong: If I was rich, I would stop working.
mistakes.right: If I were rich, I would stop working.
mistakes.note: Use were in formal contexts, especially in If I were you.

mistakes.wrong: If he knew, he will tell us.
mistakes.right: If he knew, he would tell us.
mistakes.note: In 2nd conditional result clauses, use would, not will.

quiz.question: If I ___ you, I ___ accept the offer.
quiz.explanation: 2nd conditional: If I were you + would + base verb.

quiz.question: She ___ speak better if she ___ more.
quiz.explanation: 2nd conditional: would + base verb + if + past tense.

quiz.question: What ___ you do if you ___ invisible?
quiz.explanation: 2nd conditional: would + base verb + if + were (past).

quiz.question: What is the difference between first and second conditional?
options: First = possible future, second = unreal imagination
The second conditional is more formal
quiz.explanation: 1st = real possible future, 2nd = imaginary situation opposite to reality.

tip: Memorise "If I were you" as a fixed phrase! It is the most natural way to give advice in English.

title: Relative Clauses
subtitle: Connecting clauses to describe nouns
keyPoint: Use relative pronouns (who, which, that, whose) to join two sentences into one.

cells: The man who called you is here.
The book which I read was great.
The girl whose father is a doctor...
The city where I grew up...

useCases.label: Describing people (who)
useCases.example: She is the teacher who helped me.
useCases.translation: She is the teacher who helped me.

useCases.label: Describing things (which)
useCases.example: That's the film which won the Oscar.
useCases.translation: That is the film which won the Oscar.

useCases.label: Possession (whose)
useCases.example: I know a girl whose sister is famous.
useCases.translation: I know a girl whose sister is famous.

examples.en: The woman who lives next door is a nurse.
The phone that I bought is broken.
I know a man whose wife is a chef.
Paris is the city where they got married.

mistakes.wrong: The woman which called you left.
mistakes.right: The woman who called you left.
mistakes.note: Use who, not which, for people.

mistakes.wrong: The car who I drive is red.
mistakes.right: The car which/that I drive is red.
mistakes.note: Use which/that, not who, for things.

mistakes.wrong: The man whose he works here...
mistakes.right: The man who works here...
mistakes.note: whose shows possession. 'who works' = the man working there.

quiz.question: The student ___ won the prize is from Korea.
quiz.explanation: It modifies a person (student), so use who.

quiz.question: I bought the book ___ you recommended.
quiz.explanation: It modifies a thing (book), so use which (or that).

quiz.question: She works for a company ___ products are sold worldwide.
quiz.explanation: The company's products = possession, so use whose.

quiz.question: Which relative pronoun can be omitted?
quiz.explanation: Object relative pronouns can be omitted: the book I read = the book that I read.

tip: A comma before the relative clause = non-defining (extra info only). "My brother, who lives in London, called me." (I have one brother)

title: Third Conditional
subtitle: Regrets and hypotheticals about the past
keyPoint: Use for hypothetical situations that did NOT happen in the past. If + had + p.p., would have + p.p.

cells: If + past perfect, would + base verb
If I had saved money, I would be rich now.

useCases.label: Regret about the past
useCases.example: If I had worked harder, I would have succeeded.
useCases.translation: If I had worked harder, I would have succeeded.

useCases.label: Past hypothetical
useCases.example: If she had left earlier, she wouldn't have missed the train.
useCases.translation: If she had left earlier, she wouldn't have missed the train.

useCases.label: Past affecting present
useCases.example: If he had taken that job, he would be rich now.
useCases.translation: If he had taken that job, he would be rich now.

examples.en: If I had known, I would have told you.
She would have come if she had been invited.
If we had left earlier, we wouldn't have been late.
examples.ko: 더 일찍 출발했더라면 늦지 않았을 거예요.

examples.en: He could have won if he had trained harder.
examples.ko: 더 열심히 훈련했더라면 그는 이겼을 거예요.

mistakes.wrong: If I had known, I would told you.
mistakes.right: If I had known, I would have told you.
mistakes.note: Result clause = would have + p.p. Don't omit 'have'.

mistakes.wrong: If I would have studied, I passed.
mistakes.right: If I had studied, I would have passed.
mistakes.note: Do not use would in the if-clause. Use had + p.p.

mistakes.wrong: If she hadn't come, everything is fine.
mistakes.right: If she hadn't come, everything would have been fine.
mistakes.note: The result clause needs would have + p.p.

quiz.question: If I ___ the map, I ___ lost.
quiz.explanation: If + had brought + would not have got (3rd conditional).

quiz.question: She could ___ the job if she ___ earlier.
quiz.explanation: could have got (result) + if had applied (condition).

quiz.question: What does this sentence mean? "If I had been you, I would have accepted."
options: If I had been you, I would have accepted
quiz.explanation: 3rd conditional = hypothetical past. A situation that already passed.

quiz.question: What is the core structure of the third conditional?
quiz.explanation: 3rd conditional: If + had + p.p. → would/could/might + have + p.p.

tip: The third conditional expresses regret — "If only I had..." It describes the complete opposite of what actually happened.

title: Inversion
subtitle: Reversing subject-verb order for emphasis
keyPoint: Placing certain expressions at the start inverts the subject and verb. Common in formal writing and for emphasis.

cells: So tired was she that she slept.

useCases.label: Negative emphasis
useCases.example: Never have I been so happy.
useCases.translation: I have never been so happy.

useCases.label: Formal writing
useCases.example: Not only is he smart, but he is also kind.
useCases.translation: He is not only smart but also kind.

useCases.label: Dramatic effect
useCases.example: Only then did she realise the truth.
useCases.translation: Only then did she realise the truth.

examples.en: Never have I met such an interesting person.
examples.ko: 이렇게 흥미로운 사람은 만난 적이 없어요.

examples.en: Not only did he forget, but he also didn't apologise.
examples.ko: 그는 잊었을 뿐만 아니라 사과도 하지 않았어요.

examples.en: Hardly had I sat down when the phone rang.
Only by working together can we solve this.
examples.ko: 함께 노력해야만 이 문제를 해결할 수 있어요.

mistakes.wrong: Never I have seen this.
mistakes.right: Never have I seen this.
mistakes.note: After a negative, the order is: auxiliary + subject (inversion).

mistakes.wrong: Not only he is smart but also kind.
mistakes.right: Not only is he smart but he is also kind.
mistakes.note: After Not only, invert: be/auxiliary + subject.

mistakes.wrong: Seldom she goes out.
mistakes.right: Seldom does she go out.
mistakes.note: After negative adverbs, invert with do/does/did + subject.

quiz.question: ___ I seen such a beautiful view.
quiz.explanation: Word order: Never + have + subject.

quiz.question: Not only ___ late, but he also forgot his report.
quiz.explanation: Word order: Not only + was/did/is + subject.

quiz.question: When does inversion most commonly occur?
options: When a negative adverb starts the sentence
quiz.explanation: Inversion occurs when negative adverbs like Never, Not only, Hardly, Seldom appear at the start.

quiz.question: Hardly ___ arrived when it started raining.
quiz.explanation: Word order: Hardly + had + subject: Hardly had I arrived.

tip: Inversion appears frequently in IELTS/TOEFL essays, formal speeches and literature. Do not panic when you see it in exams!

title: Subjunctive Mood
subtitle: Expressing wishes, demands and suggestions
keyPoint: The subjunctive expresses wishes, demands and suggestions. Use the base verb regardless of subject.

cells: It is important that + subject + base verb
It is essential that he be present.
I suggest that she leave now.
If I were to, Were he to...
Be that as it may / Come what may
Come what may, I will be there.

useCases.label: Demands & suggestions (that-clause)
useCases.example: The doctor insisted that he rest.
useCases.translation: The doctor insisted that he rest.

useCases.label: Formal conditionals
useCases.example: Were this to happen, we would act.
useCases.translation: If this were to happen, we would act.

useCases.label: Fixed expressions
useCases.example: Come what may, we will succeed.
useCases.translation: Come what may, we will succeed.

examples.en: It is vital that every student attend the meeting.
examples.ko: 모든 학생이 회의에 참석하는 것이 중요해요.

examples.en: I recommend that she apply for the position.
Were he to know the truth, he would be devastated.
examples.ko: 그가 진실을 안다면 큰 충격을 받을 거예요.

examples.en: The committee demanded that the report be submitted.

mistakes.wrong: It is important that he attends.
mistakes.right: It is important that he attend.
mistakes.note: In the present subjunctive, do not add -s even for 3rd person singular.

mistakes.wrong: I suggest that she leaves now.
mistakes.right: I suggest that she leave now.
mistakes.note: suggest that + base verb (subjunctive mood).

mistakes.wrong: The rule requires that everyone pays.
mistakes.right: The rule requires that everyone pay.
mistakes.note: require that + base verb.

quiz.question: It is essential that every employee ___ the training.
quiz.explanation: Present subjunctive: use the base verb regardless of subject (complete).

quiz.question: The judge ordered that the evidence ___ destroyed.
quiz.explanation: order that + be + p.p. (subjunctive passive).

quiz.question: What does "Were she to leave" mean?
quiz.explanation: Were + subject + to + verb = formal conditional meaning "If... were to...".

quiz.question: What is the difference between American and British English here?
options: The subjunctive only exists in American English
American English uses the base verb
quiz.explanation: British English prefers 'should attend'; American English uses the bare subjunctive 'attend'.

tip: Essential for IELTS C1+! Memorise 5 complete sentences with the pattern "It is important/vital/essential that..." + base verb.

title: Cleft Sentences
subtitle: Dramatically highlighting specific information
keyPoint: Cleft sentences emphasise a specific part using It is/was...that or What...is/was structures.

useCases.label: Emphasising a person
useCases.example: It was Sarah who solved the problem.
useCases.translation: It was Sarah who solved the problem.

useCases.label: Emphasising what you want
useCases.example: What I want is an honest answer.
useCases.translation: What I want is an honest answer.

useCases.label: Minimising with "all"
useCases.example: All I ask is that you be honest.
useCases.translation: All I ask is that you be honest.

examples.en: It was in Paris that they first met.
What surprised me was his reaction.
examples.ko: 저를 놀라게 한 건 그의 반응이었어요.

examples.en: It is honesty that I value most.
examples.ko: 제가 가장 소중히 여기는 건 정직이에요.

examples.en: All she wanted was to be understood.

mistakes.wrong: It was John who he called me.
mistakes.right: It was John who called me.
mistakes.note: Do not repeat the pronoun after who.

mistakes.wrong: What I need it is rest.
mistakes.right: What I need is rest.
mistakes.note: Do not repeat 'it'. What I need is already the subject.

mistakes.wrong: It is yesterday that I saw her.
mistakes.right: It was yesterday that I saw her.
mistakes.note: Use It was for past facts.

quiz.question: ___ my sister ___ bought this house.
quiz.explanation: Person (sister) + past (bought) → It was + who.

quiz.question: ___ I enjoy most is reading.
quiz.explanation: What = the thing that. "The thing I enjoy most is..."

quiz.question: What is the main purpose of cleft sentences?
quiz.explanation: Cleft sentences are used to emphasise a specific element of the sentence.

quiz.question: What type of cleft is "All I need is love"?
quiz.explanation: All + subject + verb + is + focus element = All-cleft sentence.

tip: Cleft sentences work best with stress in speech: "It was JOHN who did it (not me)." Practise the intonation — it makes you sound advanced!

title: Plural Nouns
subtitle: Talking about more than one person, place, or thing
keyPoint: Add -s or -es to most nouns to make them plural, but watch out for irregular forms like children and mice.

useCases.label: Regular Plural
useCases.example: I bought three apples at the store.

useCases.label: Ending with -es
useCases.example: She washes the dishes after dinner.

useCases.label: Irregular Plural
useCases.example: The children are playing outside.

examples.en: Two cats are sleeping on the sofa.
He packed five boxes for the move.
Many families live in this neighborhood.
Three men entered the office together.
The mice ran across the kitchen floor.

mistakes.wrong: There are three childs in the park.
mistakes.right: There are three children in the park.
mistakes.note: Child has an irregular plural form: children, not childs.

mistakes.wrong: She has two watchs.
mistakes.right: She has two watches.
mistakes.note: Words ending in -ch require -es instead of just -s.

mistakes.wrong: I saw two foots on the beach.
mistakes.right: I saw two feet on the beach.
mistakes.note: Foot changes vowels to feet in the plural form.

quiz.question: How many ___ are attending the class?
quiz.explanation: Regular nouns just take -s to make the plural form: students.

quiz.question: I saw two tiny ___ in the garden.
quiz.explanation: The plural of mouse is mice, which is an irregular form.

quiz.question: Can you bring those three ___ to the kitchen?
quiz.explanation: Nouns ending in -s add -es to form the plural: glasses.

quiz.question: Several ___ visited the museum today.
quiz.explanation: The irregular plural form of woman is women.

tip: Some nouns like sheep, fish, and deer do not change at all in the plural form (one sheep, ten sheep).

title: This / That / These / Those
subtitle: Pointing out objects based on distance and quantity
keyPoint: Use this/these for things near you, and that/those for things farther away.

useCases.label: Singular Near
useCases.example: This coffee in my hand tastes great.

useCases.label: Plural Near
useCases.example: These keys belong to my roommate.

useCases.label: Singular Far
useCases.example: Look at that bird high in the tree.

examples.en: This pen writes very smoothly.
That house across the street is old.
These shoes are very comfortable to wear.
Those mountains in the distance look blue.
Who left these papers on the table?

mistakes.wrong: These book belongs to Sarah.
mistakes.right: This book belongs to Sarah.
mistakes.note: Use this with singular nouns, and these with plural nouns.

mistakes.wrong: Look at this birds over there.
mistakes.right: Look at those birds over there.
mistakes.note: For things that are far away and plural, use those.

mistakes.wrong: I really like that shoes you are wearing.
mistakes.right: I really like those shoes you are wearing.
mistakes.note: Shoes is plural, so you must use those instead of that.

quiz.question: Could you pass me ___ pencil right next to you?
quiz.explanation: The pencil is away from the speaker (near the listener), and singular, so use that.

quiz.question: ___ apples in my basket are fresh.
quiz.explanation: Apples is plural and close to the speaker (in the basket), so use These.

quiz.question: Look at ___ stars shining in the night sky!
quiz.explanation: Stars are plural and far away, so use those.

quiz.question: ___ is my friend Daniel standing beside me.
quiz.explanation: Daniel is singular and right beside the speaker, so use This.

tip: Think of this/these as 'here' words, and that/those as 'there' words.

title: Possessive Adjectives
subtitle: Showing who owns or is connected to a noun
keyPoint: Place possessive adjectives directly before nouns to show possession or relationship.

cells: his coat, her sister, its tail

useCases.label: Personal Belongings
useCases.example: I forgot my umbrella at home.

useCases.label: Relationships
useCases.example: Her brother lives in Chicago.

useCases.label: Group Ownership
useCases.example: Our team won the championship.

examples.en: I need to recharge my phone tonight.
David is driving his new car today.
Emily called her mother this morning.
The puppy wagged its tail happily.
They parked their bicycles outside.

mistakes.wrong: The dog hurt it's paw.
mistakes.right: The dog hurt its paw.
mistakes.note: It's means 'it is'; the possessive adjective is its without an apostrophe.

mistakes.wrong: She visited she parents last weekend.
mistakes.right: She visited her parents last weekend.
mistakes.note: Use the possessive adjective her before nouns, not the subject pronoun she.

mistakes.wrong: They love they new apartment.
mistakes.right: They love their new apartment.
mistakes.note: Use their to show possession for they.

quiz.question: Lisa is doing ___ homework right now.
quiz.explanation: Lisa is female, so the corresponding possessive adjective is her.

quiz.question: We really enjoyed ___ vacation in Italy.
quiz.explanation: The subject is we, so the possessive adjective is our.

quiz.question: The cat licked ___ paws after eating.
quiz.explanation: The possessive form for an animal or object without gender specification is its (no apostrophe).

quiz.question: Paul took ___ dog for a long walk.
quiz.explanation: Paul is male singular, so his is the correct possessive adjective.

tip: Never put an apostrophe in its when showing possession—it's ALWAYS means 'it is' or 'it has'.

title: Possessive 's
subtitle: Showing ownership with an apostrophe and s
keyPoint: Add 's to singular nouns and irregular plurals, but just add an apostrophe (') after regular plural -s.

useCases.label: Singular Owner
useCases.example: Mary's laptop is on the desk.

useCases.label: Regular Plural Owner
useCases.example: The students' grades were excellent.

useCases.label: Irregular Plural Owner
useCases.example: We visited the men's clothing section.

examples.en: Sarah's car is parked outside.
The cat's bowl is completely empty.
The boys' parents arrived together.
This is the women's locker room.
Jack's brother works at a hospital.

mistakes.wrong: This is the car of Tom.
mistakes.right: This is Tom's car.
mistakes.note: In natural English, use 's for people rather than the 'of' construction.

mistakes.wrong: The dog's are barking loudly.
mistakes.right: The dogs are barking loudly.
mistakes.note: Do not use an apostrophe to form simple plurals; only use it for possession.

mistakes.wrong: The childrens' room is clean.
mistakes.right: The children's room is clean.
mistakes.note: Because children does not end in -s, add 's (children's), not s'.

quiz.question: That is my ___ jacket hanging by the door.
quiz.explanation: For one singular brother possessing a jacket, add 's: brother's.

quiz.question: The ___ toys were scattered all over the living room.
quiz.explanation: For plural babies, add just an apostrophe after the final -s: babies'.

quiz.question: We bought gifts for all the ___ party.
quiz.explanation: Children is already plural, so you add 's: children's.

quiz.question: ___ father is a famous doctor in town.
quiz.explanation: Singular proper noun Emma takes 's to show possession: Emma's.

tip: When two people share something together, add 's only to the second name (e.g., Ben and Emma's house).

title: There is / There are
subtitle: Stating what exists in a place
keyPoint: Use 'there is' with singular or uncountable nouns, and 'there are' with plural nouns.

useCases.label: Singular Object
useCases.example: There is a park near my home.

useCases.label: Plural Objects
useCases.example: There are three windows in the room.

useCases.label: Uncountable Noun
useCases.example: There is plenty of water in the bottle.

examples.en: There is a picture on the wall.
There are five people waiting in line.
There's a supermarket on the corner.
There is some coffee in the kitchen pot.
Are there any questions about the lesson?

mistakes.wrong: There have many trees in the park.
mistakes.right: There are many trees in the park.
mistakes.note: Use 'there is/are' to talk about existence, not the verb 'have'.

mistakes.wrong: There is two books on the shelf.
mistakes.right: There are two books on the shelf.
mistakes.note: Two books is plural, so you must use 'there are'.

mistakes.wrong: There are some water in the cup.
mistakes.right: There is some water in the cup.
mistakes.note: Water is uncountable and takes singular 'there is'.

quiz.question: ___ a modern computer on the study desk.
quiz.explanation: 'A modern computer' is singular, so use 'There is'.

quiz.question: ___ many students in the library today.
quiz.explanation: 'Many students' is plural, so use 'There are'.

quiz.question: Is ___ any sugar in the pantry?
quiz.explanation: In questions about existence, invert 'there is' to 'is there'.

quiz.question: ___ twelve months in a year.
quiz.explanation: 'Twelve months' is plural, so use 'There are'.

tip: In everyday spoken English, 'There's' is often contracted from 'There is' (e.g., There's a problem).

title: Countable & Uncountable Nouns
subtitle: Quantities with some, any, and a lot of
keyPoint: Countable nouns can be counted individually and have plurals, whereas uncountable nouns cannot be counted and take singular verbs.

cells: I have a lot of books.
I have a lot of water.

useCases.label: Things you can count
useCases.example: She bought three oranges and a banana.

useCases.label: Substances or concepts
useCases.example: We need to drink more water every day.

useCases.label: Indefinite quantities
useCases.example: Is there any sugar left in the bowl?

examples.en: I need some water please.
Do we have any eggs in the fridge?
She eats a lot of rice every day.
There aren't any chairs in this room.
He bought some fresh apples at the market.

mistakes.wrong: I want an advice from my teacher.
mistakes.right: I want some advice from my teacher.
mistakes.note: 'Advice' is uncountable; use 'some' or 'a piece of advice', never 'an'.

mistakes.wrong: We don't have some milk left.
mistakes.right: We don't have any milk left.
mistakes.note: Use 'any' instead of 'some' in negative statements.

mistakes.wrong: She bought two breads this morning.
mistakes.right: She bought two loaves of bread this morning.
mistakes.note: 'Bread' is uncountable, so count loaves or slices instead.

quiz.question: Do you have ___ information about the schedule?
quiz.explanation: 'Information' is uncountable, and 'any' is used in questions.

quiz.question: There are ___ pencils on the desk.
quiz.explanation: Use 'some' with countable plural nouns in positive statements.

quiz.question: He does not want ___ coffee right now.
quiz.explanation: In negative sentences with uncountable nouns, use 'any'.

quiz.question: They eat ___ fresh fruit in the morning.
quiz.explanation: 'A lot of' works naturally with uncountable nouns like 'fruit' in positive statements.

tip: If you cannot cut it into separate standalone pieces easily (like liquids, powders, or abstract ideas), treat it as uncountable.

title: Basic Prepositions (in/on/at)
subtitle: Pinpoint time and location with precision
keyPoint: Use 'at' for specific points, 'on' for surfaces and calendar days, and 'in' for enclosed spaces or longer periods.

useCases.label: Precise points
useCases.example: The train arrives at six o'clock.

useCases.label: Days and surfaces
useCases.example: The keys are lying on the kitchen table.

useCases.label: Enclosed spaces and spans
useCases.example: We moved to this city in 2021.

examples.en: Our meeting starts at nine in the morning.
She plays tennis on Saturdays with friends.
The flowers will bloom in spring.
Leave your coat on the chair over there.
They live in a small apartment downtown.

mistakes.wrong: I will see you in Monday afternoon.
mistakes.right: I will see you on Monday afternoon.
mistakes.note: Always use 'on' for specific days of the week.

mistakes.wrong: She was born at 1998.
mistakes.right: She was born in 1998.
mistakes.note: Years take the preposition 'in', not 'at'.

mistakes.wrong: We arrived on the bus stop early.
mistakes.right: We arrived at the bus stop early.
mistakes.note: Specific bus stops or meeting points use 'at'.

quiz.question: The concert begins ___ 8:30 PM tonight.
quiz.explanation: Exact clock times always require 'at'.

quiz.question: We always go hiking ___ the weekend.
quiz.explanation: In standard American English, 'on the weekend' is standard ('at the weekend' is British).

quiz.question: There is a strange stain ___ the ceiling.
quiz.explanation: A ceiling is a flat surface, so we use 'on'.

quiz.question: His birthday is ___ November.
quiz.explanation: Months without an exact day take 'in'.

tip: Think from small to large: 'at' is a point, 'on' is a line or surface, and 'in' is a 3D container or broad era.

title: Imperatives
subtitle: Giving commands, warnings, and directions
keyPoint: Form positive imperatives using the base verb with no subject, and form negative imperatives with 'Don't'.

useCases.label: Direct orders
useCases.example: Sit down and listen carefully.

useCases.label: Safety warnings
useCases.example: Watch your step on the icy stairs.

useCases.label: Step-by-step instructions
useCases.example: Turn left at the traffic light.

examples.en: Turn off the lights before you leave.
Don't run near the swimming pool.
Be quiet while the baby is sleeping.
Please pass the salt and pepper.
Don't forget to lock the back door.

mistakes.wrong: You open the door now!
mistakes.right: Open the door now!
mistakes.note: Drop the subject pronoun 'you' when giving an ordinary imperative.

mistakes.wrong: No smoke inside the building.
mistakes.right: Don't smoke inside the building.
mistakes.note: Use 'Don't + verb' for negative imperatives, not 'No + verb'.

mistakes.wrong: Not touch the hot pan.
mistakes.right: Don't touch the hot pan.
mistakes.note: Negative commands require the auxiliary 'Don't' before the base verb.

quiz.question: ___ your shoes before entering the house.
quiz.explanation: Imperatives always start with the base form of the verb.

quiz.question: ___ open that box; it is dangerous!
quiz.explanation: Negative imperatives are formed with 'Don't'.

quiz.question: Please ___ patient with the new trainee.
quiz.explanation: The base form of the verb 'be' is 'be'.

quiz.question: ___ speak so loudly in the library.
quiz.explanation: Use 'Don't' followed by the base verb for negative instructions.

tip: Add 'please' at the beginning or end of your imperative sentence to make any command sound friendly and polite.

title: Adverbs of Frequency
subtitle: How often habits and routines happen
keyPoint: Place frequency adverbs before main verbs, but immediately after the verb 'be'.

useCases.label: Daily routines
useCases.example: I always brush my teeth before going to sleep.

useCases.label: Occasional activities
useCases.example: They sometimes watch foreign movies on weekends.

useCases.label: Things that never occur
useCases.example: We never skip our morning workout.

examples.en: She always arrives five minutes early.
They are usually at home on Sunday mornings.
Mark often drinks green tea after lunch.
We sometimes cook dinner together on Friday.
I am never tired after a short walk.

mistakes.wrong: She drinks usually coffee after lunch.
mistakes.right: She usually drinks coffee after lunch.
mistakes.note: Place the frequency adverb before the main lexical verb.

mistakes.wrong: He always is tired on Monday morning.
mistakes.right: He is always tired on Monday morning.
mistakes.note: Frequency adverbs must go after the verb 'to be'.

mistakes.wrong: I don't never eat fast food.
mistakes.right: I never eat fast food.
mistakes.note: 'Never' is already negative; pairing it with 'don't' creates an incorrect double negative.

quiz.question: Tom ___ late for class.
quiz.explanation: The adverb follows the 'be' verb: 'is always'.

quiz.question: They ___ go to the gym on weekdays.
quiz.explanation: 'Usually' is the adverb of frequency that correctly modifies 'go'.

quiz.question: I ___ remember to bring my house key.
quiz.explanation: Place 'sometimes' right before the main action verb 'remember'.

quiz.question: She ___ eats spicy food because it upsets her stomach.
quiz.explanation: 'Never' expresses 0% frequency and fits the reason given.

tip: Remember: before normal verbs (I usually go), but after 'am/is/are' (I am usually).

title: Was / Were
subtitle: Talking about past states, feelings, and locations
keyPoint: Use 'was' for singular subjects (I, he, she, it) and 'were' for plural subjects and 'you'.

useCases.label: Past locations
useCases.example: We were at the beach all afternoon yesterday.

useCases.label: Past feelings or states
useCases.example: She was very happy with her exam score.

useCases.label: Describing past weather
useCases.example: It was cold and rainy last Tuesday.

examples.en: I was at the library yesterday afternoon.
They were excited about the upcoming trip.
He wasn't feeling well this morning.
We weren't surprised by the sudden news.
Were you asleep when I called your phone?

mistakes.wrong: You was late to work yesterday.
mistakes.right: You were late to work yesterday.
mistakes.note: 'You' always takes 'were', even when talking to one person.

mistakes.wrong: We was very tired last night.
mistakes.right: We were very tired last night.
mistakes.note: 'We' is plural, so it requires 'were'.

mistakes.wrong: They didn't were at home.
mistakes.right: They weren't at home.
mistakes.note: Do not use 'didn't' with 'be'; simply use 'wasn't' or 'weren't'.

quiz.question: Yesterday, Maria ___ at school because she felt sick.
quiz.explanation: Maria is singular ('she'), so the negative past of 'be' is 'wasn't'.

quiz.question: Where ___ you last night at nine o'clock?
quiz.explanation: 'You' always pairs with 'were' in past tense questions.

quiz.question: The weather ___ warm and sunny throughout the weekend.
quiz.explanation: 'The weather' is an uncountable third-person singular noun, so use 'was'.

quiz.question: Sam and Clara ___ partners on the science project.
quiz.explanation: Sam and Clara make a plural subject ('they'), requiring 'were'.

tip: 'You' is always team 'were'—never say 'you was', whether you are addressing one friend or a hundred people.

title: Object Pronouns
subtitle: Replace nouns receiving the action with me, him, her, us, and them
keyPoint: Use object pronouns after verbs and prepositions instead of repeating the noun.

cells: I saw him at the station.
Can you help us with this?

useCases.label: Direct Object
useCases.example: I called him yesterday afternoon.

useCases.label: After Prepositions
useCases.example: She is sitting next to them.

useCases.label: Indirect Object
useCases.example: Give me the book, please.

examples.en: Can you see him over there?
She gave me a wonderful present.
We invited them to our dinner party.
Listen to us carefully.
I really like her new song.

mistakes.wrong: She called I yesterday.
mistakes.right: She called me yesterday.
mistakes.note: Use the object pronoun 'me' after a verb, not the subject pronoun 'I'.

mistakes.wrong: Listen to he.
mistakes.right: Listen to him.
mistakes.note: Prepositions must be followed by object pronouns like 'him'.

mistakes.wrong: I saw they at the mall.
mistakes.right: I saw them at the mall.
mistakes.note: 'They' is a subject pronoun; use 'them' as the object.

quiz.question: Can you help ___ with these bags?
quiz.explanation: 'Help' is a verb that needs an object pronoun, so 'me' is correct.

quiz.question: I saw Sarah yesterday and spoke to ___.
quiz.explanation: 'Her' is the correct feminine singular object pronoun after the preposition 'to'.

quiz.question: Our neighbors are noisy, so we rarely talk to ___.
quiz.explanation: 'Them' is the third-person plural object pronoun.

quiz.question: Please pass the salt to ___.
quiz.explanation: Prepositions like 'to' require the object pronoun 'him'.

tip: Whenever a pronoun comes directly after a verb or a preposition, it must almost always be in its object form.

title: Can / Can't for Ability
subtitle: Talk about skills, abilities, and permission with can and can't
keyPoint: Use can or can't followed by the base form of the verb without adding -s or 'to'.

useCases.label: Physical Ability
useCases.example: He can run five kilometers easily.

useCases.label: Learned Skills
useCases.example: She can play the piano beautifully.

useCases.label: Permission
useCases.example: You can park your car here.

examples.en: She can speak Spanish fluently.
I can't swim in deep water.
Can you drive a manual car?
They can cook delicious Italian food.
We can't find our keys anywhere.

mistakes.wrong: She can to swim.
mistakes.right: She can swim.
mistakes.note: Never use 'to' after modal verbs like 'can'.

mistakes.wrong: He cans speak French.
mistakes.right: He can speak French.
mistakes.note: 'Can' never takes an '-s' ending, even with he, she, or it.

mistakes.wrong: Can you to help me?
mistakes.right: Can you help me?
mistakes.note: Use the bare infinitive without 'to' after 'can'.

quiz.question: Mark ___ ride a bicycle yet.
quiz.explanation: The negative contracted form is 'can't', followed by the base verb without 'to'.

quiz.question: ___ you speak any foreign languages?
quiz.explanation: Questions with ability invert 'can' and the subject: 'Can you speak...?'

quiz.question: My sister ___ very fast.
quiz.explanation: 'Can' is followed directly by the base verb 'run'.

quiz.question: We ___ come to the party tonight because we are busy.
quiz.explanation: 'Can't' correctly expresses an inability or impossibility.

tip: 'Can' never changes its form: I can, you can, he can, they can—always followed by a plain base verb.

title: Past Continuous
subtitle: Describe activities that were ongoing at a specific moment in the past
keyPoint: Form the past continuous with was or were plus the -ing form of the main verb.

useCases.label: Interrupted Action
useCases.example: I was cooking dinner when the phone rang.

useCases.label: Specific Past Time
useCases.example: At midnight, they were still driving.

useCases.label: Parallel Actions
useCases.example: While she was reading, he was studying.

examples.en: I was walking home when it started to rain.
They were watching a movie at eight last night.
She wasn't listening during the lecture.
What were you doing at noon yesterday?
The children were playing outside all afternoon.

mistakes.wrong: I was listen to music when you arrived.
mistakes.right: I was listening to music when you arrived.
mistakes.note: Always use the -ing form after 'was' or 'were' in continuous tenses.

mistakes.wrong: They was cooking dinner at seven.
mistakes.right: They were cooking dinner at seven.
mistakes.note: Use 'were' with plural subjects like 'they'.

mistakes.wrong: While I walked home, it was starting to rain.
mistakes.right: While I was walking home, it started to rain.
mistakes.note: Use past continuous for the longer background action and past simple for the sudden interruption.

quiz.question: At 10 PM last night, I ___ for my exam.
quiz.explanation: Use 'was studying' for a continuous ongoing activity in the past with the subject 'I'.

quiz.question: What ___ when the earthquake happened?
quiz.explanation: Invert auxiliary 'were' and subject 'you' to form past continuous questions: 'were you doing'.

quiz.question: They ___ tennis when the heavy rain began.
quiz.explanation: 'They' takes 'were', combined with the -ing verb 'playing' for background actions.

quiz.question: She ___ attention when the teacher asked her a question.
quiz.explanation: 'She' takes 'wasn't' followed by the -ing form 'paying'.

tip: Look for words like 'when' and 'while': 'while' usually introduces the longer past continuous action, whereas 'when' introduces the shorter past simple interruption.

title: Be Going To
subtitle: Express planned future intentions and predictions based on present evidence
keyPoint: Use am, is, or are going to plus a base verb for pre-planned decisions and clear future signs.

cells: rain very soon; look at the sky.

useCases.label: Prior Intentions
useCases.example: We are going to move to London next year.

useCases.label: Evidence-Based Predictions
useCases.example: Look at those dark clouds; it is going to rain.

useCases.label: Decided Plans
useCases.example: I am going to start a new diet on Monday.

examples.en: I am going to visit my sister in Paris next week.
Look at the dark clouds; it is going to rain soon.
They are going to buy a new house this spring.
She isn't going to accept that job offer.
Are you going to attend the meeting tomorrow?

mistakes.wrong: I going to study tonight.
mistakes.right: I am going to study tonight.
mistakes.note: Do not omit the helping verb 'am', 'is', or 'are'.

mistakes.wrong: She is going to buying a car.
mistakes.right: She is going to buy a car.
mistakes.note: Follow 'be going to' with the base form of the verb, not an -ing form.

mistakes.wrong: They are go to travel next week.
mistakes.right: They are going to travel next week.
mistakes.note: The fixed construction requires 'going to'.

quiz.question: Be careful! That fragile glass ___ fall off the table.
quiz.explanation: Use 'is going to' for predictions supported by immediate visual evidence.

quiz.question: We ___ meet our friends for dinner tonight.
quiz.explanation: Plural subject 'we' takes 'are going to' plus base verb for pre-planned intentions.

quiz.question: What ___ do after you graduate?
quiz.explanation: Invert 'are' and the subject 'you': 'are you going to'.

quiz.question: He ___ study medicine at university next autumn.
quiz.explanation: Singular subject 'he' matches with 'is going to'.

tip: Use 'be going to' when you have already made the plan BEFORE the moment of speaking, or when you can see physical evidence right now.

title: Will for Future
subtitle: Make instant decisions, promises, offers, and general predictions
keyPoint: Use will or won't plus the base verb for spontaneous choices, promises, and opinions about the future.

cells: I will ('ll) help you carry those bags.
I won't tell anyone your secret.
Will you come to the party tonight?

useCases.label: Instant Decisions
useCases.example: The doorbell rang; I will get it.

useCases.label: Promises & Offers
useCases.example: I promise I will call you as soon as I land.

useCases.label: Opinions & Predictions
useCases.example: I think the weather will be sunny tomorrow.

examples.en: I'll carry those heavy bags for you.
Don't worry, I won't tell anyone your secret.
I think it will be a fantastic concert.
Will you open the window, please?
Wait a minute, I will come with you.

mistakes.wrong: I will to call you later.
mistakes.right: I will call you later.
mistakes.note: Never place 'to' after modal auxiliary 'will'.

mistakes.wrong: She wills come to the meeting.
mistakes.right: She will come to the meeting.
mistakes.note: 'Will' does not take an '-s' suffix for third-person singular subjects.

mistakes.wrong: I don't will go there again.
mistakes.right: I won't go there again.
mistakes.note: The negative form of 'will' is 'will not' or 'won't', not 'don't will'.

quiz.question: Someone is knocking at the door. I ___ it!
quiz.explanation: Use 'will' ('ll) for spontaneous decisions made at the exact moment of speaking.

quiz.question: I promise I ___ forget to lock the front door.
quiz.explanation: 'Won't' is the negative form of 'will', commonly used for promises.

quiz.question: Do you think people ___ on Mars in fifty years?
quiz.explanation: Predictions based on personal opinion or belief take 'will + base verb'.

quiz.question: ___ you please help me with this heavy table?
quiz.explanation: Use 'Will you...?' to make polite requests and offers.

tip: If you decide to do something at the very moment you are speaking without a prior plan, choose 'will' rather than 'going to'.

title: Too / Enough
subtitle: Expressing excess and sufficiency with adjectives and adverbs
keyPoint: Place 'too' before an adjective to show excess, but place 'enough' after an adjective to show sufficiency.

cells: The soup is not hot enough.
It is too heavy to lift.

useCases.label: Excessive Degree
useCases.example: This jacket is too small for me.

useCases.label: Satisfactory Degree
useCases.example: He is old enough to drive a car.

useCases.label: Insufficient Degree
useCases.example: The room is not quiet enough to study.

examples.en: The coffee is too hot to drink right now.
She is tall enough to reach the top shelf.
We arrived too late to catch the train.
Are you warm enough without a coat?
The water is not clean enough for swimming.

mistakes.wrong: He is enough tall to play basketball.
mistakes.right: He is tall enough to play basketball.
mistakes.note: 'Enough' always comes AFTER the adjective, never before it.

mistakes.wrong: This car is too much fast for the city.
mistakes.right: This car is too fast for the city.
mistakes.note: Use 'too' directly with adjectives; 'too much' is only used before uncountable nouns.

mistakes.wrong: The tea is too sweet that I cannot drink it.
mistakes.right: The tea is too sweet to drink.
mistakes.note: Use 'too + adjective + to-infinitive' rather than a 'that' clause.

quiz.question: I cannot buy this watch because it is ___ expensive.
quiz.explanation: 'Too' goes directly before the adjective 'expensive' to show it exceeds what you can afford.

quiz.question: She is not fast ___ to win the gold medal.
quiz.explanation: 'Enough' must follow the adjective 'fast'.

quiz.question: The box is ___ heavy to carry alone.
quiz.explanation: The pattern 'too + adjective + to-infinitive' expresses that an excess prevents an action.

quiz.question: Is your room warm ___ for you tonight?
quiz.explanation: 'Enough' correctly follows the adjective 'warm' to ask about sufficiency.

tip: Remember: 'Too' comes BEFORE the adjective ('too cold'), but 'enough' comes AFTER ('cold enough').

title: Quantifiers
subtitle: Using much, many, few, little, and their positive forms
keyPoint: Use 'many' and 'few' with countable plural nouns, but 'much' and 'little' with uncountable nouns.

cells: a few coins / a little milk

useCases.label: Questions & Negatives
useCases.example: I do not have much time left today.

useCases.label: Small but Sufficient
useCases.example: We have a little sugar, so we can bake.

useCases.label: Scarcity & Shortage
useCases.example: He has few friends and feels lonely.

examples.en: How many books did you read last month?
She added a little milk to her morning tea.
There are a few tickets left for the concert.
Hurry up, we have very little time before departure.
Few people understand the complexity of the problem.

mistakes.wrong: There are not much cars on the road today.
mistakes.right: There are not many cars on the road today.
mistakes.note: 'Cars' is a countable plural noun, so it requires 'many', not 'much'.

mistakes.wrong: I have little friends, but we meet every weekend.
mistakes.right: I have a few friends, but we meet every weekend.
mistakes.note: 'Little' is for uncountable nouns; use 'a few' for countable plural nouns when speaking positively.

mistakes.wrong: She has a few money in her wallet.
mistakes.right: She has a little money in her wallet.
mistakes.note: 'Money' is uncountable in English and pairs with 'a little'.

quiz.question: We only have ___ minutes before the meeting begins.
quiz.explanation: 'Minutes' is countable plural and the sense is positive, so 'a few' is correct.

quiz.question: How ___ sugar do you need for this cake?
quiz.explanation: 'Sugar' is an uncountable noun, so questions ask with 'how much'.

quiz.question: I am so sad because I have ___ opportunities here.
quiz.explanation: 'Opportunities' is countable plural, and the negative tone (almost none) requires 'few'.

quiz.question: Can you lend me ___ cash for the bus?
quiz.explanation: 'Cash' is uncountable, so 'a little' is used to request a small positive amount.

tip: 'A few' and 'a little' have the letter 'a' and mean 'some' (positive); without 'a', they mean 'hardly any' (negative).

title: Indefinite Pronouns
subtitle: Referring to non-specific people, things, and places
keyPoint: Indefinite pronouns take singular verbs, with 'some-' used in positive statements and 'any-' in questions or negatives.

useCases.label: Positive Assertions
useCases.example: Somebody left their keys on the dining table.

useCases.label: Questions & Negatives
useCases.example: Did anybody call while I was outside?

useCases.label: Total Absence
useCases.example: There is nothing to worry about.

examples.en: Somebody is knocking at the front door.
I looked everywhere, but I found nothing.
Does anyone know the correct answer?
We did not go anywhere special during vacation.
Everything is ready for the presentation tomorrow.

mistakes.wrong: Everybody are ready for the test.
mistakes.right: Everybody is ready for the test.
mistakes.note: Indefinite pronouns ending in -body, -one, or -thing always take a singular verb.

mistakes.wrong: I did not see nobody at the park.
mistakes.right: I did not see anybody at the park.
mistakes.note: Avoid double negatives; use 'anybody' after a negative auxiliary verb.

mistakes.wrong: She wants to buy something cheap somewhere?
mistakes.right: Does she want to buy anything cheap somewhere?
mistakes.note: Use 'any-' forms in standard open questions instead of 'some-'.

quiz.question: Listen carefully! ___ is trying to open the back gate.
quiz.explanation: 'Someone' refers to an unknown person in an affirmative sentence.

quiz.question: There was ___ in the office; it was completely empty.
quiz.explanation: 'Nobody' conveys the negative meaning of total absence in an affirmative clause.

quiz.question: Everyone in the classroom ___ waiting quietly.
quiz.explanation: 'Everyone' is grammatically singular and requires the singular verb 'is'.

quiz.question: Did you buy ___ delicious at the bakery?
quiz.explanation: Use 'anything' for an object in an interrogative sentence.

tip: Even though 'everyone' feels plural in meaning, always treat it as singular grammatically: 'Everyone has', never 'Everyone have'.

title: Have To
subtitle: Talking about external obligation, rules, and lack of necessity
keyPoint: Use 'have to' for obligations created by rules or situations, and 'don't have to' to show there is no obligation.

cells: She has to wear a uniform.
do / does not have to + verb
You do not have to pay.
Do / Does + subject + have to + verb?
Do we have to leave now?
I had to walk home yesterday.

useCases.label: Legal & School Rules
useCases.example: Drivers have to stop at the red light.

useCases.label: Absence of Obligation
useCases.example: Tomorrow is Sunday, so I do not have to wake up early.

useCases.label: Past Necessity
useCases.example: We had to wait an hour for the doctor.

examples.en: Every passenger has to show a valid ticket.
You do not have to finish this report today.
Does your brother have to work on weekends?
examples.highlight: Does your brother have to work

examples.en: We had to cancel the picnic because of heavy rain.
I have to wake up at six every morning.

mistakes.wrong: He has not to work on Saturdays.
mistakes.right: He does not have to work on Saturdays.
mistakes.note: 'Have to' uses ordinary verb question and negative patterns with do/does, not 'has not to'.

mistakes.wrong: You do not have to touch the hot stove!
mistakes.right: You must not touch the hot stove!
mistakes.note: 'Don't have to' means it is not necessary, whereas prohibition requires 'must not'.

mistakes.wrong: Yesterday I must go to the clinic.
mistakes.right: Yesterday I had to go to the clinic.
mistakes.note: 'Must' has no past tense form; use 'had to' for obligations in the past.

quiz.question: Tom ___ wear glasses when he reads books.
quiz.explanation: Third-person singular subjects ('Tom') require 'has to'.

quiz.question: The museum is free, so you ___ buy an entry ticket.
quiz.explanation: 'Do not have to' expresses that an action is unnecessary.

quiz.question: ___ you have to travel often for your job?
quiz.explanation: Questions with 'have to' in the present simple begin with 'Do' or 'Does'.

quiz.question: Because the bus broke down, we ___ walk two miles.
quiz.explanation: 'Had to' is the correct past form for external necessity.

tip: Careful! 'You don't have to' means you can if you want, but you don't need to. 'You must not' means it is forbidden.

title: Gerunds & Infinitives: Basics
subtitle: Choosing between verb-ing and to + base verb
keyPoint: Certain verbs are followed by gerunds (-ing) and others by to-infinitives, while prepositions always take gerunds.

useCases.label: Enjoyment & Habits (Gerunds)
useCases.example: He avoids driving during rush hour.

useCases.label: Plans & Desires (Infinitives)
useCases.example: We hope to visit Canada next summer.

useCases.label: Following Prepositions
useCases.example: She is interested in learning Spanish.

examples.en: I enjoy playing tennis on Saturday mornings.
They decided to move to a new apartment.
She promised to call me after landing.
Would you mind closing the window, please?
He is very good at solving difficult puzzles.

mistakes.wrong: I enjoy to swim in the ocean.
mistakes.right: I enjoy swimming in the ocean.
mistakes.note: 'Enjoy' is always followed by a gerund (-ing), never an infinitive.

mistakes.wrong: She decided buying the blue dress.
mistakes.right: She decided to buy the blue dress.
mistakes.note: 'Decide' must be followed by a to-infinitive.

mistakes.wrong: He left without to say goodbye.
mistakes.right: He left without saying goodbye.
mistakes.note: Any verb that directly follows a preposition (such as 'without') must be in the -ing form.

quiz.question: We hope ___ our final exams next week.
quiz.explanation: 'Hope' is followed by the to-infinitive ('to pass').

quiz.question: Have you finished ___ your bedroom yet?
quiz.explanation: 'Finish' takes a gerund (-ing) as its object.

quiz.question: Are you interested in ___ with our team?
quiz.explanation: The preposition 'in' must be followed by a gerund ('working').

quiz.question: They promised ___ us as soon as they arrive.
quiz.explanation: 'Promise' is followed by a to-infinitive ('to call').

tip: Easy rule: Preposition + verb ALWAYS equals '-ing' (e.g., 'thank you for helping', 'good at drawing').

title: Like + -ing
subtitle: Talking about likes, dislikes, and hobbies
keyPoint: Use a verb ending in -ing after like, love, enjoy, and hate to express general preferences.

useCases.label: Hobbies & Free Time
useCases.example: He loves playing the guitar on weekends.

useCases.label: Dislikes & Chores
useCases.example: I hate washing the dishes after dinner.

useCases.label: General Preferences
useCases.example: Do you like listening to podcasts?

examples.en: She likes cooking Italian food with her friends.
We love traveling abroad during the summer holidays.
He hates doing laundry on Sunday evenings.
I really enjoy watching foreign films at night.
Do you like running in the park before work?

mistakes.wrong: She likes to swimming every morning.
mistakes.right: She likes swimming every morning.
mistakes.note: Do not combine 'to' with the '-ing' form.

mistakes.wrong: I enjoy to listen to classical music.
mistakes.right: I enjoy listening to classical music.
mistakes.note: 'Enjoy' must be followed by a gerund (-ing), never by a to-infinitive.

mistakes.wrong: He hates run in the winter.
mistakes.right: He hates running in the winter.
mistakes.note: Use the -ing form after 'hate' when expressing an activity you dislike.

quiz.question: Sam hates ___ the train during rush hour.
quiz.explanation: After 'hate', use the -ing form 'taking' to talk about an unpleasant activity.

quiz.question: Do you enjoy ___ new languages?
quiz.explanation: The verb 'enjoy' is always followed by a gerund ending in -ing.

quiz.question: My parents really like ___ long walks in the countryside.
quiz.explanation: We use the verb phrase 'going for' (verb + -ing) directly after 'like'.

quiz.question: I love ___ breakfast in bed on Sundays.
quiz.explanation: Use the gerund 'eating' after 'love' to describe an enjoyable habit.

tip: Remember spelling rules when adding -ing: drop a silent -e (make → making) and double a single final consonant after a short vowel (run → running).

title: Basic Conjunctions
subtitle: Connecting thoughts with and, but, because, and so
keyPoint: Use conjunctions to show addition (and), contrast (but), reason (because), or result (so) between clauses.

cells: I studied hard, but I failed.
She left early because she was tired.
It rained heavily, so we stayed home.

useCases.label: Giving Reasons
useCases.example: He wore a thick coat because the weather was freezing.

useCases.label: Showing Results
useCases.example: The train was delayed, so we arrived late to the meeting.

useCases.label: Contrasting Facts
useCases.example: She wanted to buy the dress, but it was too expensive.

examples.en: She called me yesterday, but I did not hear the phone ring.
We stayed at home because the storm was very dangerous.
He forgot his wallet, so he could not buy any lunch.
I turned on the computer and started writing my essay.
They were tired because they walked ten miles today.

mistakes.wrong: Because it was raining, so we took an umbrella.
mistakes.right: Because it was raining, we took an umbrella.
mistakes.note: Do not use 'because' and 'so' together in the same sentence.

mistakes.wrong: I was hungry because I ordered a pizza.
mistakes.right: I was hungry, so I ordered a pizza.
mistakes.note: Use 'so' to state the result, and 'because' to explain the reason.

mistakes.wrong: She is clever so friendly.
mistakes.right: She is clever and friendly.
mistakes.note: Use 'and' to connect two positive, similar characteristics.

quiz.question: I wanted to go to the concert, ___ all tickets were sold out.
quiz.explanation: 'But' introduces a contrast between wanting to go and the tickets being sold out.

quiz.question: He missed the morning bus, ___ he walked all the way to work.
quiz.explanation: 'So' shows the result or consequence of missing the bus.

quiz.question: Maria stayed in bed all day ___ she had a severe headache.
quiz.explanation: 'Because' introduces the reason for staying in bed.

quiz.question: We went to the supermarket ___ bought fresh vegetables for salad.
quiz.explanation: 'And' joins two chronological and complementary actions.

tip: Think of 'because' as answering 'Why?' (Cause) and 'so' as answering 'What happened next?' (Effect).

title: Irregular Past Verbs
subtitle: Common past simple forms without -ed
keyPoint: Irregular verbs do not add -ed in the past simple; their unique forms must be learned by heart.

useCases.label: Completed Past Actions
useCases.example: Yesterday I went to the post office and sent a letter.

useCases.label: Past Experiences
useCases.example: We saw an incredible documentary on TV last night.

useCases.label: Daily Routines in the Past
useCases.example: She had toast and coffee for breakfast this morning.

examples.en: She went to the grocery store after finishing her work.
We had a wonderful dinner at the new Italian restaurant.
They saw their favorite teacher at the library yesterday.
He made a delicious chocolate cake for his brother's birthday.
I did not see anyone waiting at the platform.

mistakes.wrong: We goed to the shopping center last night.
mistakes.right: We went to the shopping center last night.
mistakes.note: 'Go' is irregular; its past simple form is 'went', never 'goed'.

mistakes.wrong: She didn't had any money in her purse.
mistakes.right: She didn't have any money in her purse.
mistakes.note: After 'didn't', always return the verb to the base infinitive form ('have').

mistakes.wrong: He maked an appointment yesterday.
mistakes.right: He made an appointment yesterday.
mistakes.note: The past simple of 'make' is 'made'.

quiz.question: Last weekend, we ___ a lot of delicious food at the festival.
quiz.explanation: The past simple of the irregular verb 'eat' is 'ate'.

quiz.question: I ___ my keys on the kitchen table before I left.
quiz.explanation: 'Left' is the irregular past simple form of 'leave'.

quiz.question: Did you ___ Clara at the party yesterday?
quiz.explanation: In past questions with 'Did', the main verb remains in the base form 'see'.

quiz.question: David ___ an interesting book about ancient history last week.
quiz.explanation: The past form of 'read' is spelled 'read' (pronounced like 'red').

tip: When forming negatives and questions in the past, use didn't / did + base verb; do not use the past form twice!

title: Adverbs of Manner
subtitle: Describing how an action is performed
keyPoint: Adverbs of manner describe how an action happens and usually come after the main verb or object.

useCases.label: Describing Speed & Pace
useCases.example: The turtle moved slowly across the garden lawn.

useCases.label: Describing Performance
useCases.example: He plays the violin extremely well after years of practice.

useCases.label: Describing Volume & Tone
useCases.example: Please speak quietly because the baby is sleeping.

examples.en: The team solved the difficult math problem quickly.
She plays tennis very well because she practices daily.
He drives fast on the highway but carefully in town.
The old woman walked slowly down the icy sidewalk.
The children laughed happily while playing with the puppy.

mistakes.wrong: She speaks English very good.
mistakes.right: She speaks English very well.
mistakes.note: 'Good' is an adjective. Use the adverb 'well' to modify the verb 'speaks'.

mistakes.wrong: He drives his car fastly.
mistakes.right: He drives his car fast.
mistakes.note: 'Fast' is an irregular adverb and does not take -ly.

mistakes.wrong: They worked hardly all day to finish.
mistakes.right: They worked hard all day to finish.
mistakes.note: 'Hard' means with great effort; 'hardly' means almost not at all.

quiz.question: He finished the examination ___ and checked his answers twice.
quiz.explanation: The adverb 'quickly' modifies how he finished the examination.

quiz.question: Our teacher explained the difficult grammar rules very ___.
quiz.explanation: Use the adverb 'clearly' to describe the action of explaining.

quiz.question: She dances ___ and won first place in the competition.
quiz.explanation: 'Beautifully' is the manner adverb describing how she dances.

quiz.question: Carlos plays the piano remarkably ___, surprising everyone.
quiz.explanation: The adverb form of 'good' is the irregular word 'well'.

tip: Never place an adverb of manner between a transitive verb and its direct object: say 'He opened the door quietly', not 'He opened quietly the door'.

title: Present Perfect Continuous
subtitle: Actions starting in the past and continuing right now
keyPoint: Use have/has + been + -ing to emphasize the duration of an ongoing action that started in the past.

useCases.label: Duration up to Now
useCases.example: I have been living in this apartment for three years.

useCases.label: Recent Ongoing Activity with Evidence
useCases.example: Her hands are dirty because she has been working in the garden.

useCases.label: Temporary Situations
useCases.example: He has been staying with a friend until he finds a flat.

examples.en: She has been studying for the medical exam since 8 AM.
They have been waiting at the bus stop for forty minutes.
Why are you out of breath? Have you been running in the park?
It has been raining continuously since yesterday afternoon.
We have been trying to contact customer service all day.

mistakes.wrong: I am living here for five years.
mistakes.right: I have been living here for five years.
mistakes.note: Use the present perfect continuous (not present continuous) with 'for' to show duration up to now.

mistakes.wrong: She has been knowing him since childhood.
mistakes.right: She has known him since childhood.
