mistakes.note: Stative verbs like 'know', 'believe', or 'like' cannot be used in continuous tenses.

mistakes.wrong: They have been work on this project since Monday.
mistakes.right: They have been working on this project since Monday.
mistakes.note: The main verb must take the -ing form after 'have been'.

quiz.question: How long ___ you ___ English at this school?
quiz.explanation: Use 'have you been studying' to ask about the duration of an ongoing learning action.

quiz.question: He is exhausted because he ___ heavy boxes all afternoon.
quiz.explanation: 'Has been lifting' explains his current state of fatigue through a prolonged recent activity.

quiz.question: Look at the wet pavement! It ___ for hours.
quiz.explanation: The present perfect continuous 'has been raining' emphasizes ongoing action leading to a present result.

quiz.question: We ___ this new software since nine o'clock this morning.
quiz.explanation: With the subject 'We' and duration marker 'since nine o'clock', use 'have been testing'.

tip: Use 'since' with a specific starting point in time (since 2020, since 9 AM) and 'for' with a duration or length of time (for three hours, for two days).

title: Past Perfect
subtitle: Talking about an action that happened before another point in the past
keyPoint: Use 'had' plus the past participle to show that one past event occurred before another past event.

cells: She had left when I arrived.

useCases.label: Earlier Past Action
useCases.example: The train had already departed when we reached the platform.

useCases.label: Cause and Effect in Past
useCases.example: He was tired because he had worked all night.

useCases.label: Unrealized Past Intentions
useCases.example: I had hoped to see her, but she was away.

examples.en: When Sarah arrived at the cinema, the film had already started.
He couldn't buy a ticket because he had forgotten his wallet.
By the time we woke up, the snow had stopped falling.
They had never visited London before their trip last winter.
I recognized him immediately because I had met him years ago.

mistakes.wrong: When I arrived, the train already left.
mistakes.right: When I arrived, the train had already left.
mistakes.note: Use the past perfect for the event that happened first.

mistakes.wrong: She had ate breakfast before going to work.
mistakes.right: She had eaten breakfast before going to work.
mistakes.note: Always pair 'had' with the past participle (V3), not the past simple form.

mistakes.wrong: I had seen him yesterday at five.
mistakes.right: I saw him yesterday at five.
mistakes.note: Do not use the past perfect for a single past action with a specific time stamp; use past simple.

quiz.question: By the time the rescue team arrived, the hikers ___ shelter.
quiz.explanation: The past perfect 'had found' is required because finding shelter happened before the team arrived.

quiz.question: She failed the test because she ___ the material.
quiz.explanation: Negative past perfect is formed using 'hadn't' + past participle ('studied').

quiz.question: I realized that I ___ my keys inside the apartment.
quiz.explanation: 'Had left' describes the earlier past action that was realized later.

quiz.question: ___ you already eaten when they invited you out?
quiz.explanation: Questions in the past perfect start with 'Had' + subject + past participle.

tip: Think of the past perfect as looking back from a point in the past, just like present perfect looks back from now.

title: Reported Speech
subtitle: Sharing what someone else said without quoting them word-for-word
keyPoint: When reporting speech with a past reporting verb, shift the original tenses one step back into the past.

cells: 'I am cold' -> She said she was cold.
'We are leaving' -> They said they were leaving.
'I lost it' -> He said he had lost it.
'I will call' -> She said she would call.

useCases.label: Reporting Statements
useCases.example: Mark said that he was planning to move abroad.

useCases.label: Reporting Questions
useCases.example: She asked me if I knew the answer.

useCases.label: Reporting Requests/Commands
useCases.example: The teacher told us to open our books.

examples.en: David said he was feeling unwell and wanted to go home.
She told me that she had never tried sushi before.
The manager said they would announce the results tomorrow.
Elena asked if I could help her with the project.
My brother mentioned that he had bought a new bicycle.

mistakes.wrong: She said me that she was tired.
mistakes.right: She told me that she was tired.
mistakes.note: 'Tell' requires an indirect object (told me), whereas 'say' does not take a personal object directly.

mistakes.wrong: He said that he will come tomorrow.
mistakes.right: He said that he would come tomorrow.
mistakes.note: When the reporting verb is in the past ('said'), shift 'will' to 'would'.

mistakes.wrong: She asked me where did I live.
mistakes.right: She asked me where I lived.
mistakes.note: Reported questions use normal statement word order, not question inversion.

quiz.question: Tom said, 'I need some help.' -> Tom said that he ___ some help.
quiz.explanation: Present simple 'need' shifts back to past simple 'needed'.

quiz.question: She told us that she ___ to Spain the following week.
quiz.explanation: 'Will' backshifts to 'would' in reported speech after a past reporting verb.

quiz.question: He asked me ___ I had seen his keys anywhere.
quiz.explanation: Use 'if' or 'whether' to report yes/no questions.

quiz.question: The doctor ___ me to get more rest.
quiz.explanation: 'Told' takes a direct personal object followed by an infinitive: 'told me to get'.

tip: Remember to also shift pronouns and time words: 'now' becomes 'then', and 'yesterday' becomes 'the day before'.

title: Gerund vs Infinitive (Meaning Change)
subtitle: Choosing between -ing and to-infinitive when verb meaning changes
keyPoint: Certain verbs like 'remember', 'stop', and 'forget' completely alter their meaning depending on whether they are followed by a gerund or an infinitive.

cells: Pause in order to do something else
Keep in mind a duty or task
Lose memory of a past event
Fail to do a necessary task
Make an effort to achieve something difficult

useCases.label: Interrupting an Action
useCases.example: He stopped smoking five years ago.

useCases.label: Pausing for a Purpose
useCases.example: We stopped to buy some coffee on our way.

useCases.label: Recalling Past Experiences
useCases.example: I remember locking the front door before leaving.

examples.en: On the way home, she stopped to buy fresh flowers.
The doctor told him that he must stop drinking sugary soda.
Please remember to turn off the lights before you leave.
I clearly remember meeting him at the conference last year.
Don't forget to lock the garage door tonight.

mistakes.wrong: I stopped to smoke because it was bad for my health.
mistakes.right: I stopped smoking because it was bad for my health.
mistakes.note: 'Stop doing' means quitting a habit; 'stop to do' means pausing an activity in order to smoke.

mistakes.wrong: Remember locking the door before you leave.
mistakes.right: Remember to lock the door before you leave.
mistakes.note: Use 'remember + to-infinitive' for duties and actions you still need to complete.

mistakes.wrong: I tried to turn the key the other way, but nothing happened.
mistakes.right: I tried turning the key the other way, but nothing happened.
mistakes.note: Use 'try + gerund' when experimenting with a different method to see if it works.

quiz.question: While driving through the mountains, we stopped ___ photographs of the sunset.
quiz.explanation: 'Stop to do' indicates pausing an action in order to perform another action.

quiz.question: I will never forget ___ the Grand Canyon for the very first time.
quiz.explanation: 'Forget + gerund' refers to losing the memory of a past event.

quiz.question: Did you remember ___ milk on your way back from work?
quiz.explanation: 'Remember + infinitive' means not forgetting to do a planned task.

quiz.question: If you have trouble sleeping, try ___ a cup of warm chamomile tea.
quiz.explanation: 'Try + gerund' means testing or experimenting with a solution to see if it works.

tip: Gerunds often point backward to memories or continuous habits, while to-infinitives point forward to duties or future goals.

title: Used To
subtitle: Describing past habits and states that are no longer true today
keyPoint: Use 'used to + base verb' to express past repeated actions or long-term states that have ceased in the present.

cells: I used to live in Paris.
She didn't use to like spicy food.
Did you use to play the piano?

useCases.label: Past Habits
useCases.example: He used to jog every single morning before breakfast.

useCases.label: Past States
useCases.example: This building used to be a bustling cinema.

useCases.label: Changes Over Time
useCases.example: I didn't use to drink coffee, but now I love it.

examples.en: My grandfather used to walk five miles to school every day.
We used to live near the beach before moving to the city.
She didn't use to enjoy reading, but now she reads constantly.
Did you use to play football when you were in high school?
There used to be a lovely park right on this street corner.

mistakes.wrong: I didn't used to like vegetables.
mistakes.right: I didn't use to like vegetables.
mistakes.note: After 'didn't', use the base form 'use to' without the final '-d'.

mistakes.wrong: I used to going swimming every weekend.
mistakes.right: I used to go swimming every weekend.
mistakes.note: 'Used to' expressing past habits takes a base verb (bare infinitive), not a gerund.

mistakes.wrong: I use to wake up at six every day now.
mistakes.right: I usually wake up at six every day now.
mistakes.note: 'Used to' only refers to the past; use 'usually' with present simple for current habits.

quiz.question: When we were children, we ___ spend our summers by the lake.
quiz.explanation: 'Used to' + base verb expresses a past repeated routine.

quiz.question: He ___ have long hair, but he shaved it off last month.
quiz.explanation: 'Used to' expresses a past state that is no longer true.

quiz.question: ___ you use to cycle to school every morning?
quiz.explanation: Questions with 'use to' use the auxiliary 'Did' in the past simple.

quiz.question: She didn't ___ enjoy jazz, but now she attends concerts regularly.
quiz.explanation: In negative sentences with 'didn't', the spelling drops the 'd': 'use to'.

tip: Do not confuse 'used to do' (past habit) with 'be used to doing' (being accustomed to something in the present).

title: Tag Questions
subtitle: Turning statements into confirmation checks using mini-questions
keyPoint: Add a short auxiliary question at the end of a statement, using an opposite polarity (positive statement + negative tag, or vice versa).

cells: You are coming tonight, aren't you?
She hasn't called yet, has she?
I'm right about this, aren't I?
Let's grab a coffee, shall we?

useCases.label: Checking Information
useCases.example: You locked the front door, didn't you?

useCases.label: Inviting Agreement
useCases.example: It's a gorgeous day outside, isn't it?

useCases.label: Softening Requests
useCases.example: Pass me that salt shaker, will you?

examples.en: You don't eat meat, do you?
She is moving to Toronto next month, isn't she?
They had already left before the rain started, hadn't they?
We can park our car right here, can't we?
I am invited to the wedding, aren't I?

mistakes.wrong: You like chocolate, isn't it?
mistakes.right: You like chocolate, don't you?
mistakes.note: Match the auxiliary verb of the main clause; present simple verbs require 'do/does'.

mistakes.wrong: She didn't call you, didn't she?
mistakes.right: She didn't call you, did she?
mistakes.note: A negative statement must be followed by a positive tag.

mistakes.wrong: I'm late, amn't I?
mistakes.right: I'm late, aren't I?
mistakes.note: The standard tag question for 'I am' in negative form is 'aren't I?'.

quiz.question: Your brother works at the hospital, ___?
quiz.explanation: With a third-person singular present simple verb ('works'), use the auxiliary 'doesn't he'.

quiz.question: They haven't finished the project yet, ___?
quiz.explanation: A negative statement with 'haven't' requires a positive tag: 'have they?'.

quiz.question: You will help us move this heavy sofa, ___?
quiz.explanation: The negative tag for 'will' is 'won't you?'.

quiz.question: Let's take a short break now, ___?
quiz.explanation: Suggestions beginning with 'Let's' conventionally take the tag 'shall we?'.

tip: A falling intonation on the tag means you are sure and just seeking agreement; a rising intonation means it is a real question.

title: So vs Such
subtitle: Adding emphasis to adjectives, adverbs, and nouns
keyPoint: Use 'so' directly before an adjective or adverb, but use 'such' before a noun phrase.

cells: It is such a hot day.
No article with plural or uncountable
She spoke so fast that I got lost.

useCases.label: Direct Adjective Emphasis
useCases.example: You are so kind to help us with the move.

useCases.label: Noun Phrase Emphasis
useCases.example: We had such a wonderful time at the concert.

useCases.label: Cause and Effect
useCases.example: The music was so loud that the windows shook.

examples.en: The sunset was so beautiful yesterday evening.
She told such an inspiring story during her lecture.
They made such delicious cookies for the party.
He walked so quickly that nobody could keep up.
It was such bad weather that the flight was canceled.

mistakes.wrong: It was a so good film.
mistakes.right: It was such a good film.
mistakes.note: Never put 'a' before 'so'; use 'such a' before an adjective with a singular countable noun.

mistakes.wrong: She is such smart.
mistakes.right: She is so smart.
mistakes.note: 'Smart' is an adjective alone, so it requires 'so' instead of 'such'.

mistakes.wrong: They have so great ideas.
mistakes.right: They have such great ideas.
mistakes.note: Use 'such' before plural noun phrases, not 'so'.

quiz.question: The exam was ___ difficult that almost everyone ran out of time.
quiz.explanation: 'Difficult' is an adjective standing alone, so we use 'so' to introduce the result clause.

quiz.question: He is ___ polite young man whenever we speak.
quiz.explanation: 'Polite young man' is a singular countable noun phrase, requiring 'such a'.

quiz.question: They prepared ___ delicious meals for the festival.
quiz.explanation: 'Delicious meals' is a plural noun phrase, which takes 'such' without an article.

quiz.question: Why did you run ___ fast down the corridor?
quiz.explanation: 'Fast' is an adverb here, so it takes 'so'.

tip: Check the very end of the phrase: if a noun is present at the end, choose 'such' (e.g., 'such a long trip'); if it ends on an adjective, choose 'so' (e.g., 'so long').

title: Reflexive Pronouns
subtitle: Actions that turn back on the subject
keyPoint: Use reflexive pronouns when the subject and the object of the verb refer to the exact same person or thing.

cells: I cut myself while chopping onions.
The cat cleaned itself in the sun.
She prefers to travel by herself.

useCases.label: Subject Equals Object
useCases.example: Be careful with that knife or you will hurt yourself.

useCases.label: Emphasis (Intensive)
useCases.example: The manager herself answered the phone.

useCases.label: Solitary Action
useCases.example: He painted the entire apartment by himself.

examples.en: I taught myself how to play the piano during the summer.
She looked at herself in the mirror before heading out.
We prepared ourselves for a very difficult exam.
The children built the treehouse all by themselves.
The software updates itself automatically every Tuesday.

mistakes.wrong: Please contact John or myself if you have questions.
mistakes.right: Please contact John or me if you have questions.
mistakes.note: Use the object pronoun 'me' here, because the subject is 'you' (implied), not 'I'.

mistakes.wrong: They bought the tickets for theirselves.
mistakes.right: They bought the tickets for themselves.
mistakes.note: 'Theirselves' does not exist in standard English; the correct plural form is 'themselves'.

mistakes.wrong: I feel myself very tired today.
mistakes.right: I feel very tired today.
mistakes.note: Verbs like 'feel', 'relax', and 'concentrate' are not used with reflexive pronouns in English.

quiz.question: Did you make this whole dinner all by ___?
quiz.explanation: Addressing one person doing something alone requires 'by yourself'.

quiz.question: Emma blamed ___ for the mistake on the report.
quiz.explanation: Emma is both the doer and receiver of the blame, so the reflexive pronoun 'herself' is required.

quiz.question: We promised ___ that we would exercise every morning.
quiz.explanation: The subject is 'we', so the matching reflexive pronoun is 'ourselves'.

quiz.question: The computer shut ___ down after the update installed.
quiz.explanation: The computer is an inanimate subject, so it refers back to 'itself'.

tip: To test whether a reflexive pronoun is used correctly as an emphatic word, remove it: 'The chef (himself) cooked this' still makes complete sense.

title: Phrasal Verbs: Introduction
subtitle: Combining verbs with particles to create new meanings
keyPoint: A phrasal verb pairs a base verb with a preposition or adverb to produce an idiomatic meaning distinct from the single words.

cells: Never give up on your dreams.
Please turn off the lights before you leave.
I am looking for my keys.
We found out the truth yesterday.

useCases.label: Everyday Daily Routines
useCases.example: I wake up at seven and get up immediately.

useCases.label: Separable with Pronoun Objects
useCases.example: The radio was noisy, so she turned it off.

useCases.label: Inseparable Combinations
useCases.example: Who will look after the children while you are away?

examples.en: He decided to give up sugar for one month.
Could you pick up some milk on your way home?
She needs to find out what time the train arrives.
Please put on your warm jacket before going outside.
We ran out of coffee early this morning.

mistakes.wrong: Please turn off it before sleeping.
mistakes.right: Please turn it off before sleeping.
mistakes.note: When a separable phrasal verb takes a pronoun object ('it', 'them'), the pronoun MUST go between the verb and particle.

mistakes.wrong: I look forward to hear from you soon.
mistakes.right: I look forward to hearing from you soon.
mistakes.note: In 'look forward to', 'to' is a preposition, so it must be followed by a gerund (-ing).

mistakes.wrong: She woke herself up at 6 am.
mistakes.right: She woke up at 6 am.
mistakes.note: 'Wake up' is normally intransitive and does not take a reflexive pronoun unless causing someone else to wake.

quiz.question: I don't know this word, so I will ___ in the dictionary.
quiz.explanation: Pronoun objects must sit between separable parts: 'look it up'.

quiz.question: Can you ___ the cat while we are on holiday?
quiz.explanation: 'Look after' means to care for someone or something.

quiz.question: We must hurry because we are running ___ time.
quiz.explanation: 'Run out of' means to deplete your supply of something, such as time or fuel.

quiz.question: He was very sick last week, but he managed to ___ it.
quiz.explanation: 'Get over' means to recover from an illness or emotional setback.

tip: Whenever you learn a phrasal verb, test whether a pronoun splits it: 'turn it off' (separable) vs 'look after it' (inseparable).

title: Both, Either, and Neither
subtitle: Talking about two people, things, or choices
keyPoint: 'Both' refers to two together (+ plural verb), 'either' refers to one or the other, and 'neither' means not one nor the other.

cells: not the first and not the second

useCases.label: Affirming Both Items
useCases.example: Both Sarah and her brother love hiking in the mountains.

useCases.label: Offering Alternatives
useCases.example: You can have either tea or coffee with your breakfast.

useCases.label: Double Negative Sense
useCases.example: Neither answer was correct on the test.

examples.en: Both sisters play the violin exceptionally well.
Either you apologize now, or we will not leave.
Neither jacket fits me comfortably.
Both of my parents work at the university.
Neither the teacher nor the students were ready for the drill.
examples.highlight: Neither the teacher nor the students were

mistakes.wrong: Neither of them didn't come to the party.
mistakes.right: Neither of them came to the party.
mistakes.note: 'Neither' already carries a negative meaning, so adding 'didn't' creates an incorrect double negative.

mistakes.wrong: Both Tom or Alex can drive.
mistakes.right: Either Tom or Alex can drive.
mistakes.note: Pair 'both' with 'and', and 'either' with 'or'.

mistakes.wrong: Both my brother is tall.
mistakes.right: Both my brothers are tall.
mistakes.note: 'Both' must modify a plural noun and takes a plural verb.

quiz.question: ___ my parents are teachers at the local high school.
quiz.explanation: 'Both' is used for two people and pairs with the plural verb 'are'.

quiz.question: You can choose ___ the chocolate cake or the apple pie.
quiz.explanation: The correlative conjunction that pairs with 'or' is 'either'.

quiz.question: Neither of the keys ___ the front door.
quiz.explanation: In standard formal English, 'neither of' takes a singular verb: 'unlocks'.

quiz.question: She liked ___ the dress nor the skirt that was on sale.
quiz.explanation: The correlative conjunction that pairs with 'nor' is 'neither'.

tip: Remember the first letters: Either goes with Or (E...O), and Neither matches Nor with an N (N...N).

title: Stative Verbs
subtitle: Verbs expressing states rather than actions
keyPoint: Stative verbs describe thoughts, feelings, senses, and possession, and are generally not used in continuous (-ing) tenses.

useCases.label: Mental States
useCases.example: I know the answer to your question.

useCases.label: Emotional Reactions
useCases.example: He wants a glass of water right now.

useCases.label: Dual Meaning Verbs
useCases.example: I think you are right (belief) vs I am thinking about it (mental action).

examples.en: I know your brother from our college days.
This suitcase belongs to the passenger in front of us.
She wants a new computer for her graphic design course.
The flowers smell wonderful in the garden today.
We believe that your team will win the championship.

mistakes.wrong: I am knowing the answer right now.
mistakes.right: I know the answer right now.
mistakes.note: 'Know' is a stative verb of cognition and is not used in the continuous form, even for 'right now'.

mistakes.wrong: This phone is belonging to me.
mistakes.right: This phone belongs to me.
mistakes.note: Possession verbs like 'belong' are always expressed in simple tenses.

mistakes.wrong: Are you wanting another cup of tea?
mistakes.right: Do you want another cup of tea?
mistakes.note: 'Want' expresses a desire or state, requiring the present simple question form 'Do you want'.

quiz.question: Listen carefully! I ___ what you mean.
quiz.explanation: 'Understand' is a stative verb of cognition, so use the present simple: 'don't understand'.

quiz.question: That vintage sports car ___ to my grandfather.
quiz.explanation: 'Belong' is stative and never continuous; the third-person singular takes 'belongs'.

quiz.question: Why ___ at the picture so closely?
quiz.explanation: 'Look at' is a deliberate physical action here, not a state of appearance, so continuous is correct.

quiz.question: Right now, she ___ three different languages fluently.
quiz.explanation: 'Know' cannot be continuous even with 'Right now'; she takes 'knows'.

tip: Some verbs switch meanings: 'have a car' (possession = stative) versus 'having lunch' (eating = active action that allows -ing).

title: Talking About the Future
subtitle: Choosing between will, be going to, and present continuous
keyPoint: Use 'will' for spontaneous decisions, 'be going to' for intentions or visible evidence, and the present continuous for confirmed arrangements.

cells: I think it will rain later.
Look at those dark clouds; it is going to rain.
Fixed plans with other people or times
I am meeting Sarah for lunch on Friday.

useCases.label: Instant Decisions
useCases.example: The phone is ringing; I will answer it.

useCases.label: Intentions & Evidence
useCases.example: We are going to buy a new house next year.

useCases.label: Arranged Appointments
useCases.example: He is flying to London tomorrow morning.

examples.en: I will carry that heavy bag for you.
She is going to study medicine at university.
They are having dinner with the director tonight.
Be careful, you are going to drop those glasses!
Don't worry, I will remember to lock the door.

mistakes.wrong: I will meet my dentist at 3 PM tomorrow.
mistakes.right: I am meeting my dentist at 3 PM tomorrow.
mistakes.note: Use the present continuous for fixed appointments already arranged with someone else.

mistakes.wrong: Look at that car! It will crash!
mistakes.right: Look at that car! It is going to crash!
mistakes.note: Use 'be going to' when present physical evidence shows something is about to happen.

mistakes.wrong: Wait, I am going to open the door for you.
mistakes.right: Wait, I will open the door for you.
mistakes.note: Use 'will' for offers and spontaneous decisions made at the moment of speaking.

quiz.question: Someone is knocking at the door. — Don't worry, I ___ it!
quiz.explanation: We use 'will' for spontaneous decisions made right at the moment of speaking.

quiz.question: We have booked the tickets. We ___ to Paris next Tuesday.
quiz.explanation: The present continuous expresses a confirmed, fixed arrangement in the future.

quiz.question: Look at those dark storm clouds! It ___ heavily.
quiz.explanation: 'Be going to' is required when observable evidence indicates an immediate future outcome.

quiz.question: Have you decided on a holiday? — Yes, we ___ explore Norway.
quiz.explanation: Use 'be going to' for plans and intentions decided before the moment of speaking.

tip: Ask yourself: 'Did I plan this before speaking?' If yes, pick 'going to' or present continuous; if you decided just now, use 'will'.

title: Mixed Conditionals
subtitle: Connecting past actions to present results and vice versa
keyPoint: Mixed conditionals combine different timeframes, most commonly linking a past condition (had done) with a present result (would do).

useCases.label: Past Event affecting Now
useCases.example: If I had taken that job, I would live in Tokyo now.

useCases.label: Permanent Trait affecting Past
useCases.example: If I were braver, I would have defended him yesterday.

useCases.label: Past Choice altering Status
useCases.example: If they had won the match, they would be champions today.

examples.en: If I had gone to medical school, I would be a doctor today.
examples.highlight: had gone to medical school, I would be

examples.en: If she were not so stubborn, she would have listened to your advice.
examples.highlight: were not so stubborn, she would have listened

examples.en: If we had left earlier, we would not be stuck in traffic right now.
examples.highlight: had left earlier, we would not be

examples.en: If he spoke fluent German, he would have applied for that Berlin position.
examples.highlight: spoke fluent German, he would have applied

examples.en: If you had eaten breakfast, you would not feel exhausted now.
examples.highlight: had eaten breakfast, you would not feel

mistakes.wrong: If I had studied harder, I would have been a doctor now.
mistakes.right: If I had studied harder, I would be a doctor now.
mistakes.note: Use 'would + infinitive' (not 'would have been') because the result describes your present status.

mistakes.wrong: If I would have known, I would be happy.
mistakes.right: If I had known, I would be happy.
mistakes.note: Never put 'would' inside the 'if' condition clause.

mistakes.wrong: If I was you, I would have accepted the contract.
mistakes.right: If I were you, I would have accepted the contract.
mistakes.note: Use the subjunctive 'were' rather than 'was' in unreal hypothetical conditional clauses.

quiz.question: If I ___ that flight yesterday, I would be sitting on a tropical beach right now.
quiz.explanation: The condition happened in the past, so we require the past perfect ('had caught').

quiz.question: If Mark spoke French, he ___ the tourists who asked for directions this morning.
quiz.explanation: A general present ability ('spoke') altering a past completed action requires 'would have + V3'.

quiz.question: If she had saved more money last year, she ___ able to afford this apartment today.
quiz.explanation: Because 'today' refers to a current state resulting from a past choice, use 'would be'.

quiz.question: If we ___ so much yesterday, we wouldn't feel so tired today.
quiz.explanation: A past action influencing a present feeling requires the past perfect ('hadn't walked') in the if-clause.

tip: Look at time markers: words like 'yesterday' or 'last night' require past forms, while 'now' or 'today' signal simple forms.

title: Wish / If Only
subtitle: Expressing regrets, desires for change, and dissatisfaction
keyPoint: Step one tense back into the past when expressing wishes: use Past Simple for the present, Past Perfect for past regrets, and 'would' for annoying habits.

cells: Desire for a different present reality
Regret about an unchangeable past event

useCases.label: Present Unreal Desire
useCases.example: I wish I had more free time during weekdays.

useCases.label: Past Regret
useCases.example: If only I had studied harder for that exam.

useCases.label: Complaining about Habit
useCases.example: I wish you would stop tapping your pen on the desk.

examples.en: I wish I were taller so I could play basketball well.
If only we had booked our hotel rooms earlier.
She wishes she didn't have to work on Saturday morning.
I wish it would stop raining so we could walk outside.
He wishes he had told the truth from the beginning.

mistakes.wrong: I wish I will pass my driving test tomorrow.
mistakes.right: I hope I pass my driving test tomorrow.
mistakes.note: Use 'hope' (not 'wish') for possible and realistic future outcomes.

mistakes.wrong: I wish I would have more money right now.
mistakes.right: I wish I had more money right now.
mistakes.note: Do not use 'would' for current desires or states; shift present states to the Past Simple.

mistakes.wrong: I wish I didn't say those words yesterday.
mistakes.right: I wish I hadn't said those words yesterday.
mistakes.note: Regrets regarding past actions demand the Past Perfect ('hadn't said').

quiz.question: I feel terrible today. I wish I ___ so much cake last night.
quiz.explanation: Regretting an action completed in the past ('last night') takes the Past Perfect ('hadn't eaten').

quiz.question: This apartment is far too small. If only we ___ a bigger living room.
quiz.explanation: Wishing for a different present state requires shifting to the Past Simple ('had').

quiz.question: Your music is giving me a headache. I wish you ___ the volume down!
quiz.explanation: Expressing irritation and asking someone else to alter their behavior takes 'would + infinitive'.

quiz.question: He lives in an isolated village. He wishes he ___ closer to his friends.
quiz.explanation: Wishing for a continuing present state takes the past subjunctive or continuous ('were living').

tip: Never say 'I wish I would' about yourself; use 'would' only when you want another person or external circumstance to change.

title: Future Perfect & Future Continuous
subtitle: Looking back from the future and picturing actions in progress
keyPoint: Use the Future Continuous (will be doing) for ongoing actions at a future point, and Future Perfect (will have done) for actions completed before a future deadline.

cells: at 8 PM, this time next week
by Friday, by the time you arrive
Action will be finished before a deadline
Emphasizing ongoing duration up to a point

useCases.label: In Progress at Future Time
useCases.example: This time tomorrow, I will be flying over the Atlantic.

useCases.label: Completed Prior to Deadline
useCases.example: By next month, the builders will have finished the bridge.

useCases.label: Polite Routine Inquiry
useCases.example: Will you be using the printer this afternoon?

examples.en: Don't call at seven because we will be eating dinner.
By the end of the year, she will have written her entire novel.
At noon tomorrow, the engineers will be running safety tests.
They will have lived in Spain for twenty years by December.
By the time the train arrives, we will have waited an hour.

mistakes.wrong: By next year, I will finish my degree.
mistakes.right: By next year, I will have finished my degree.
mistakes.note: Sentences introduced with 'by + time marker' require the Future Perfect to indicate prior completion.

mistakes.wrong: When you arrive, I will cook dinner.
mistakes.right: When you arrive, I will be cooking dinner.
mistakes.note: If you want the cooking to be in progress upon their arrival, use the Future Continuous.

mistakes.wrong: By the time she will arrive, we will be ready.
mistakes.right: By the time she arrives, we will be ready.
mistakes.note: In subordinate time clauses with 'by the time' or 'when', use the Present Simple, not 'will'.

quiz.question: Do not call between 2 and 4 PM; I ___ an important client.
quiz.explanation: The meeting will be in progress during that specific time bracket, needing the Future Continuous.

quiz.question: By 2030, scientists ___ a cure for this rare condition.
quiz.explanation: The preposition 'by' indicates an action that will be completed before that specified future limit.

quiz.question: By the time our parents arrive, we ___ the entire house.
quiz.explanation: 'By the time' signals a deadline before which the cleaning will be completely finished.

quiz.question: This time next week, we ___ on a sunny beach in Greece.
quiz.explanation: 'This time next week' specifies an action taking place and continuing at that exact moment in the future.

tip: Think of the word 'by' as an alarm clock deadline: it almost always calls for the Future Perfect ('will have done').

title: Modal Perfect
subtitle: Deductions, regrets, and assumptions about past events
keyPoint: Combine modal verbs with 'have + past participle' to speculate, deduce certainty, or express criticism regarding past situations.

cells: She must have forgotten her keys.
Certainty that an event was impossible
He can't have stolen the money; he was away.
You should have checked the oil level.
They might have taken the earlier train.

useCases.label: Strong Past Deduction
useCases.example: The grass is wet; it must have rained overnight.

useCases.label: Past Regret or Mistake
useCases.example: I should have listened to your financial advice.

useCases.label: Past Impossibility
useCases.example: She couldn't have seen me because I was in Rome.

examples.en: The lights are off; they must have left the building.
He can't have passed the exam without revising at all.
You should have called me when your flight landed safely.
They might have missed the announcement due to the noise.
I shouldn't have eaten that third slice of cake.

mistakes.wrong: He mustn't have stolen the car; he was with me all night.
mistakes.right: He can't have stolen the car; he was with me all night.
mistakes.note: Use 'can't have' (or 'couldn't have') to express past impossibility; 'mustn't have' is rarely used for deductions.

mistakes.wrong: You should have went to the doctor immediately.
mistakes.right: You should have gone to the doctor immediately.
mistakes.note: Always pair modal perfects with the past participle (gone), never the past simple form (went).

mistakes.wrong: She could left her purse in the coffee shop.
mistakes.right: She could have left her purse in the coffee shop.
mistakes.note: Speculations regarding the past require the auxiliary 'have' directly following the modal verb.

quiz.question: The bakery shelves are empty. Customers ___ everything early this morning.
quiz.explanation: A near-certain past deduction based on visible proof uses 'must have + past participle'.

quiz.question: Tom was with me in Boston all day yesterday, so he ___ the window in Chicago.
quiz.explanation: 'Can't have + past participle' expresses that a past event was logically impossible.

quiz.question: I failed the driving examination. I ___ more with my instructor.
quiz.explanation: 'Should have + past participle' communicates regret or an unfulfilled advisable action in the past.

quiz.question: Where is my coat? — I don't know, you ___ it on the bus.
quiz.explanation: 'Might have left' indicates an uncertain past possibility.

tip: Remember that the negative of 'must have done' (deduction) is 'can't have done', never 'mustn't have done'.

title: Reported Questions
subtitle: Reporting inquiries using statement word order without question marks
keyPoint: Reported questions use standard affirmative word order (subject + verb) without auxiliary 'do/does/did' or question marks.

cells: She inquired if I was ready.
They asked what time it started.
We asked whether we could help.

useCases.label: Wh- Questions
useCases.example: She asked what I wanted for dinner.

useCases.label: Yes/No Questions with If
useCases.example: He wanted to know if the train was delayed.

useCases.label: Formal Enquiries with Whether
useCases.example: The officer inquired whether we held valid passports.

examples.en: She asked where I had bought that jacket.
He asked if we could meet on Tuesday.
They inquired how long the flight would take.
examples.highlight: how long the flight would take

examples.en: I wondered whether the museum was open on Mondays.
The receptionist asked what time our appointment was.

mistakes.wrong: She asked me where did I live.
mistakes.right: She asked me where I lived.
mistakes.note: Do not retain question inversion or auxiliary 'did' in reported questions.

mistakes.wrong: He asked if was I tired.
mistakes.right: He asked if I was tired.
mistakes.note: The word order must follow Subject + Verb, not Verb + Subject.

mistakes.wrong: They asked what time does the train arrive?
mistakes.right: They asked what time the train arrived.
mistakes.note: Remove the question mark and shift the tense backward when reporting past speech.

quiz.question: He asked me where ___ during my vacation in Rome.
quiz.explanation: Reported questions require statement word order (Subject + Verb) without the auxiliary 'did'.

quiz.question: The manager wanted to know whether we ___ the contract yet.
quiz.explanation: In indirect speech anchored in the past ('wanted'), the present perfect shifts back to past perfect ('had signed').

quiz.question: She asked ___ any dietary restrictions.
quiz.explanation: Yes/no questions take 'if' or 'whether' followed by standard subject-verb order in the past tense.

quiz.question: They inquired how much the entire repair ___ cost.
quiz.explanation: 'Will' shifts back to 'would' in reported past contexts.

tip: Never place a question mark at the end of an indirect or reported question unless the entire sentence itself is a direct question (e.g., 'Could you tell me where he went?').

title: Advanced Participle Constructions
subtitle: Condensing clauses with present, past, and perfect participle structures
keyPoint: Participle clauses provide concise, formal alternatives to adverbial or relative clauses, sharing an implied subject with the main clause.

cells: Shocked by the news, she wept.
Because she was shocked by the news...
Having been warned, they took care.

useCases.label: Prior Action (Perfect Participle)
useCases.example: Having completed the audit, the team presented the findings.

useCases.label: Cause & Effect (Past Participle)
useCases.example: Exhausted by the long trek, the hikers rested by the river.

useCases.label: Simultaneous Action (Present Participle)
useCases.example: Walking along the shore, she gathered smooth pebbles.

examples.en: Having lost all his savings, he was forced to declare bankruptcy.
Surrounded by reporters, the prime minister refused to answer further questions.
Not knowing which path to choose, we consulted the trail map.
Having been rejected twice, the proposal was completely rewritten.
Glancing over her shoulder, the agent quickened her pace.

mistakes.wrong: Walking down the street, the trees looked gorgeous.
mistakes.right: Walking down the street, I noticed the trees looked gorgeous.
mistakes.note: Avoid dangling participles; the subject of the participle must match the subject of the main clause.

mistakes.wrong: Having ate his lunch, he returned to work.
mistakes.right: Having eaten his lunch, he returned to work.
mistakes.note: Use the past participle form after 'having' (having + eaten, not ate).

mistakes.wrong: Not have received the letter, she called the bank.
mistakes.right: Not having received the letter, she called the bank.
mistakes.note: Form negative perfect participles with 'Not having + past participle'.

quiz.question: ___ all relevant documents, the lawyer submitted the formal petition.
quiz.explanation: The perfect participle 'Having examined' clearly denotes an action completed prior to the submission.

quiz.question: ___ by high taxation, several international firms relocated abroad.
quiz.explanation: The passive meaning requires the past participle 'Threatened'.

quiz.question: ___ the severe weather warnings, the sailors ventured out into open water.
quiz.explanation: The present active participle 'Ignoring' conveys the ongoing attitude/action of the sailors.

quiz.question: ___ twice before, the suspect knew not to make any unprompted remarks.
quiz.explanation: A passive prior action requires 'Having been' plus the past participle 'cautioned'.

tip: Always check for dangling participles by asking: 'Who is actually performing the action of the -ing/-ed verb?' Ensure that exact noun is the main clause subject.

title: Nominalization
subtitle: Transforming verbs and adjectives into academic abstract nouns
keyPoint: Nominalization converts verbs and adjectives into nouns to establish an objective, dense, and formal academic tone.

useCases.label: Academic Objectivity
useCases.example: The reduction in emissions improved urban air quality.

useCases.label: Condensing Prior Arguments
useCases.example: This assumption forms the cornerstone of modern economic modeling.

useCases.label: Shifting Focus from Agent to Event
useCases.example: The cancellation of the summit surprised European delegates.

examples.en: The rapid expansion of the digital economy reshaped traditional commerce.
Careful examination of the artifact revealed unexpected microscopic engravings.
Her reluctance to sign the treaty caused considerable diplomatic friction.
The sudden deterioration of weather conditions grounded all outbound aircraft.
A clear understanding of statistical variation prevents flawed scientific conclusions.

mistakes.wrong: The implementing of the policy took six months.
mistakes.right: The implementation of the policy took six months.
mistakes.note: Use standard derived nouns (implementation) instead of awkward gerund phrases with articles.

mistakes.wrong: Her intense of curiosity surprised the researchers.
mistakes.right: Her intensity of curiosity surprised the researchers.
mistakes.note: 'Intense' is an adjective; the abstract nominal form is 'intensity'.

mistakes.wrong: The government decided to analyze the situation led to reforms.
mistakes.right: The government's analysis of the situation led to reforms.
mistakes.note: A whole verbal clause cannot serve ungrammatically as a subject noun without proper nominalization.

quiz.question: The sudden ___ of the currency triggered widespread financial panic.
quiz.explanation: 'Depreciation' is the formal abstract noun derived from the verb 'depreciate'.

quiz.question: Scholars questioned the ___ of the newly discovered parchment.
quiz.explanation: The noun form derived from the adjective 'authentic' is 'authenticity'.

quiz.question: The ___ of rare minerals across the valley remains unevenly distributed.
quiz.explanation: 'Accumulation' functions as the head noun needed for the subject of the sentence.

quiz.question: Diplomats praised the bilateral ___ reached between both border nations.
quiz.explanation: 'Accommodation' is the standard noun indicating a reached compromise or settlement.

tip: While nominalization strengthens academic prose, excessive use creates dense, unreadable text. Balance abstract nouns with precise active verbs.

title: Discourse Markers
subtitle: Guiding reader interpretation with formal transitional devices
keyPoint: Conjunctive discourse markers (e.g., moreover, nevertheless, consequently) signal logical relationships across independent sentences and formal clauses.

useCases.label: Reinforcing Arguments (Addition)
useCases.example: The method is cost-effective; furthermore, it reduces hazardous emissions.

useCases.label: Counterbalancing (Concession)
useCases.example: Funding remained scarce; nevertheless, the researchers persevered.

useCases.label: Logical Outcomes (Result)
useCases.example: Oil supplies dwindled; consequently, retail fuel costs spiked.

examples.en: The survey sample was unrepresentative; consequently, the findings cannot be generalized.
Initial trials yielded ambiguous results. Nevertheless, the laboratory secured further grants.
The engine consumes minimal fuel; moreover, its maintenance costs are exceptionally low.
Public transport was suspended; hence, many workers stayed home.
The legislation has drawn fierce criticism; nonetheless, Parliament is expected to pass it.

mistakes.wrong: The hypothesis was flawed, moreover the experiment failed.
mistakes.right: The hypothesis was flawed; moreover, the experiment failed.
mistakes.note: Conjunctive adverbs like 'moreover' cannot join independent clauses with just a comma (run-on sentence).

mistakes.wrong: Despite the rain was heavy, nevertheless we departed.
mistakes.right: Although the rain was heavy, we departed.
mistakes.note: Do not stack subordinating conjunctions ('despite/although') with conjunctive adverbs ('nevertheless') in the same relation.

mistakes.wrong: He had no experience. Consequently however, he was hired.
mistakes.right: He had no experience. Nevertheless, he was hired.
mistakes.note: 'Consequently' signals cause, whereas hiring an inexperienced candidate is an unexpected contrast requiring 'nevertheless'.

quiz.question: The laboratory was severely understaffed; ___, they met all deadlines.
quiz.explanation: 'Nevertheless' marks an unexpected contrast or concession between lack of staff and meeting deadlines.

quiz.question: The software is intuitive to navigate. ___, it offers robust encryption tools.
quiz.explanation: 'Moreover' supplies supplementary supporting information (addition).

quiz.question: The company infringed copyright regulations; ___, it was fined millions of dollars.
quiz.explanation: 'Consequently' indicates that the fine was the direct logical result of the infringement.

quiz.question: Renewable energy adoption has accelerated; ___, storage remains an engineering hurdle.
quiz.explanation: 'However' provides the necessary contrast to highlight the remaining challenge.

tip: When starting a sentence with 'Moreover', 'Nevertheless', or 'Consequently', always follow the adverb immediately with a comma.

title: Hedging
subtitle: Softening assertions and adjusting commitment in academic discourse
keyPoint: Hedging uses tentative verbs, probability modals, and mitigating adverbs to avoid absolute generalizations and maintain academic precision.

cells: The treatment could yield minor improvements.
Students tend to underestimate revision time.
This is arguably the most influential study.
It is suggested that sample sizes be widened.

useCases.label: Qualifying General Trends
useCases.example: Older demographics tend to favor broadcast news over social media platforms.

useCases.label: Expressing Cautionary Evidence
useCases.example: The latest metrics seem to suggest a mild economic contraction.

useCases.label: Presenting Bold Claims Tentatively
useCases.example: This breakthrough is arguably the most significant discovery of the decade.

examples.en: The preliminary clinical trials appear to indicate a positive patient response.
Antibiotic resistance is arguably one of the greatest perils facing public health.
Children raised in bilingual households tend to develop heightened metalinguistic awareness.
The experimental methodology was somewhat unconventional, yet it yielded reproducible data.
It could be argued that previous research prioritized urban settlements disproportionately.

mistakes.wrong: This experiment definitely proves that all people react identically.
mistakes.right: These findings suggest that people may react similarly under controlled conditions.
mistakes.note: Avoid dogmatic words like 'definitely proves' and 'all' in academic claims.

mistakes.wrong: The participants were somewhat completely exhausted.
mistakes.right: The participants were somewhat exhausted.
mistakes.note: Do not combine mitigating adverbs ('somewhat') with absolute adjectives ('completely').

mistakes.wrong: It appears that the data is arguably proving the theory.
mistakes.right: The data appears to support the theory.
mistakes.note: Do not over-hedge by stacking 'appears', 'arguably', and 'suggests' clumsily in a single clause.

quiz.question: The figures ___ suggest an impending surge in international travel demand.
quiz.explanation: 'Seem to' hedges the claim, presenting the assertion as a tentative interpretation rather than an absolute fact.

quiz.question: This novel is ___ the author's most nuanced exploration of grief.
quiz.explanation: 'Arguably' allows the author to defend a subjective literary evaluation with appropriate nuance.

quiz.question: First-year undergraduates ___ experience acute stress during examination periods.
quiz.explanation: 'Tend to' correctly qualifies a general behavioral tendency without overgeneralizing to every student.

quiz.question: The newly introduced regulations proved ___ counterproductive in urban districts.
quiz.explanation: 'Somewhat' tempers the severity of the evaluative adjective 'counterproductive'.

tip: Distinguish between epistemic stance (degree of certainty) and evidentiality (source of evidence). Effective hedgers use both to invite scholarly dialogue rather than dogmatic consensus.

title: Ellipsis & Substitution
subtitle: Streamline discourse by omitting understood elements or substituting key phrases
keyPoint: Ellipsis removes words that are clear from context, while substitution replaces repeated words with forms like 'one', 'so', or auxiliary verbs.

cells: I didn't buy the red shirt; I bought the blue one.
They asked him to resign, and he did so immediately.
Can you attend tomorrow? — I certainly can.
I wanted to go abroad, but I couldn't afford to.

useCases.label: Avoiding Noun Repetition
useCases.example: These new headphones sound far clearer than my old ones.

useCases.label: Formal Action Replacement
useCases.example: The committee advised everyone to stay, and the members did so.

useCases.label: Reduced Infinitive Clauses
useCases.example: She offered to help review the contract, but I preferred not to.

examples.en: If you need a reliable pen, take this one on my desk.
Management asked the staff to report early, and many did so.
Will you visit the gallery this weekend? — I might.
He asked me to close the window, so I decided to.
She believes the proposal will pass, and I think so too.

mistakes.wrong: Which jacket do you prefer? — The blue.
mistakes.right: Which jacket do you prefer? — The blue one.
mistakes.note: Singular countable nouns cannot stand alone with just an adjective; use 'one' as a pronoun.

mistakes.wrong: She didn't want to attend the party, but she had to attend.
mistakes.right: She didn't want to attend the party, but she had to.
mistakes.note: Native discourse prefers stranded 'to' rather than repeating the full infinitive verb phrase.

mistakes.wrong: He dropped his coffee and did so by accident.
mistakes.right: He dropped his coffee and did it by accident.
mistakes.note: 'Do so' typically substitutes deliberate actions, whereas accidental events take 'do it' or 'do that'.

quiz.question: I would love to travel to Antarctica, but I simply cannot afford ___.
quiz.explanation: In reduced infinitives, the stranded particle 'to' stands for the entire verb phrase ('afford to travel').

quiz.question: All visitors must register their vehicles upon entry, and failure to ___ will result in a fine.
quiz.explanation: 'Do so' is the formal substitution for repeating a previously stated deliberate action ('register their vehicles').

quiz.question: These boots are completely worn out, so I need to purchase new ___.
quiz.explanation: Plural countable nouns are substituted with 'ones'.

quiz.question: Do you believe inflation will ease by autumn? — I certainly hope ___.
quiz.explanation: Verbs of belief and anticipation (hope, think, believe, suppose) use 'so' to substitute a positive that-clause.

tip: Reserve 'do so' for formal writing and deliberate actions; in everyday speech, native speakers prefer 'do it' or 'do that'.

title: Fronting
subtitle: Position complements and adverbials first to create cohesion and strong focus
keyPoint: Fronting shifts an object, complement, or adverbial to the absolute beginning of a clause to highlight contrasts or link smoothly with preceding ideas.

cells: This crucial detail we must never overlook.
Furious though he was, he kept his composure.
Behind the ancient fortress stood a modern observatory.
Rarely have I witnessed such dedication.

useCases.label: Thematic Continuity
useCases.example: We discussed three candidates. The third applicant we hired immediately.

useCases.label: Dramatic Contrast
useCases.example: Generous she may be, but gullible she certainly is not.

useCases.label: Descriptive Setting
useCases.example: Through the valley ran an icy mountain stream.

examples.en: That peculiar painting I could never understand.
Talented as she is, she remains extremely humble.
Next to the fireplace sat an imposing leather armchair.
Much of the original manuscript we have managed to restore.
Strange though it seemed, nobody contested the unexpected verdict.

mistakes.wrong: This point we must consider it carefully.
mistakes.right: This point we must consider carefully.
mistakes.note: Do not leave a duplicate pronoun ('it') behind when fronting an object.

mistakes.wrong: Under the bridge a homeless man slept was.
mistakes.right: Under the bridge slept a homeless man.
mistakes.note: Locative fronting causes subject-verb inversion without auxiliary insertion for intransitive verbs.

mistakes.wrong: Brilliant although he is, he lacks experience.
mistakes.right: Brilliant though he is, he lacks experience.
mistakes.note: Fronted adjective concessions take 'though' or 'as', not 'although'.

quiz.question: We examined several alternatives, but the final option ___ without hesitation.
quiz.explanation: Object fronting retains standard Subject + Verb word order without inserting auxiliary verbs or redundant pronouns.

quiz.question: Exhausted ___ they were, the hikers pressed on until sunset.
quiz.explanation: The pattern [Adjective + though / as + Subject + Verb] expresses concession.

quiz.question: At the summit of the mountain ___ an ancient bronze bell.
quiz.explanation: Fronted prepositional phrases of place trigger full subject-verb inversion with intransitive verbs of position/motion.

quiz.question: Most of these preliminary objections ___ anticipate during the design phase.
quiz.explanation: Direct object fronting does not trigger auxiliary inversion; standard declarative order (Subject + Modal + Verb) is maintained.

tip: Use fronting sparingly; overusing it in academic prose sounds theatrical rather than authoritative.

title: Reduced Relative Clauses
subtitle: Condense relative clauses into streamlined participle or adjective phrases
keyPoint: A relative clause can be reduced by deleting the relative pronoun and the verb 'be', turning the clause into a present or past participle phrase.

cells: The man who is waving at us
The policy that was approved yesterday
Anyone who is suitable for the role

useCases.label: Active Descriptions
useCases.example: Scientists investigating the anomaly published their findings.

useCases.label: Passive Descriptions
useCases.example: Articles submitted after midnight will not be accepted.

useCases.label: Postpositive Adjectives
useCases.example: Please report any luggage left unattended in the terminal.

examples.en: The architect designing the tower won an international prize.
Goods imported from abroad are subject to import duties.
Students wishing to apply must submit their portfolios today.
The funds allocated for this project have already run out.
We need all documents relevant to this legal inquiry.

mistakes.wrong: The woman who standing near the doorway is the CEO.
mistakes.right: The woman standing near the doorway is the CEO.
mistakes.note: When reducing, you must drop BOTH the relative pronoun and the auxiliary verb; never retain the pronoun alone.

mistakes.wrong: The report writing by the analyst contained several errors.
mistakes.right: The report written by the analyst contained several errors.
mistakes.note: Passive clauses reduce to past participles (-ed / V3), not present participles (-ing).

mistakes.wrong: The technician whom we consulted him gave useful advice.
mistakes.right: The technician consulted gave useful advice.
mistakes.note: Do not keep personal pronouns when transforming into a reduced participial structure.

quiz.question: Any parcel ___ hazardous materials will be confiscated at security.
quiz.explanation: 'Containing' reduces the active clause 'which contains hazardous materials' using a present participle.

quiz.question: The guidelines ___ by the board must be observed by all employees.
quiz.explanation: 'Stipulated' functions as a passive reduced participle meaning 'which were stipulated by the board'.

quiz.question: Passengers ___ to board the vessel should assemble at Gate 4.
quiz.explanation: Active ongoing action reduces to the present participle (-ing): 'Passengers (who are) preparing'.

quiz.question: All personnel ___ in the incident gave statements to the police.
quiz.explanation: 'Involved' is the reduced passive participle for 'personnel who were involved'.

tip: Only subject relative clauses can be reduced to participle phrases; if the pronoun is an object (whom/which), reduction is not possible.

title: Causative (Have/Get)
subtitle: Arranging for someone else to do things for you
keyPoint: Use 'have' or 'get' followed by an object and a past participle when someone else performs a service for you.

cells: More informal; implies effort or persuasion
The boss had us rewrite the report.
Instructing or requiring someone to do a task
I got my friend to help me move.
Persuading or convincing someone to do an action

useCases.label: Professional Services
useCases.example: We are having the house painted next week.

useCases.label: Accidents & Misfortunes
useCases.example: He had his passport stolen at the airport.

useCases.label: Persuading Someone
useCases.example: She finally got her brother to clean the garage.

examples.en: I need to have my watch repaired before the trip.
She got her hair cut at a brand new salon downtown.
We had our roof damaged during the severe storm last night.
The manager had the assistant prepare the presentation slides.
Can you get someone to translate this document into Spanish?

mistakes.wrong: I cut my hair yesterday at the salon.
mistakes.right: I had my hair cut yesterday at the salon.
mistakes.note: Saying 'I cut my hair' means you physically held the scissors and did it yourself.

mistakes.wrong: I got the mechanic inspect my brakes.
mistakes.right: I got the mechanic to inspect my brakes.
mistakes.note: Use 'get + person + TO-infinitive', whereas 'have + person' uses the bare infinitive.

mistakes.wrong: She had her laptop fix by a technician.
mistakes.right: She had her laptop fixed by a technician.
mistakes.note: When the object receives the action, you must use the past participle ('fixed', not 'fix').

quiz.question: I don't know how to wire a plug, so I will have an electrician ___ it.
quiz.explanation: With 'have + person', use the bare infinitive without 'to': 'have an electrician do it'.

quiz.question: She finally managed to get her son ___ his homework.
quiz.explanation: The causative pattern with 'get + person' requires the full infinitive with 'to'.

quiz.question: Mark had his wallet ___ while riding the crowded subway.
quiz.explanation: Use 'have + object + past participle' to describe an unfortunate event that happens to someone's property.

quiz.question: We really need to ___ our air conditioner serviced before summer begins.
quiz.explanation: 'Get' fits the structure 'get + object + past participle' after the modal infinitive 'need to'.

tip: 'Get something done' often implies that there was some difficulty or effort involved in organizing the task compared to 'have something done'.

title: Participle Clauses
subtitle: Combining clauses concisely using -ing and -ed forms
keyPoint: Participle clauses economize language by replacing full adverbial or relative clauses when both clauses share the same subject.

cells: Feeling exhausted, she went to bed.
Shocked by the news, he sat down.
Because he was shocked by the news...
Having finished work, we went home.
Having been warned, they were careful.

useCases.label: Simultaneous Actions
useCases.example: Whistling a cheerful tune, he walked down the street.

useCases.label: Sequential Actions
useCases.example: Having locked the front door, she ran to catch her bus.

useCases.label: Causes & Reasons
useCases.example: Knowing very little Italian, Marcus relied heavily on a translation app.

examples.en: Waiting for the bus, Sarah noticed a stray kitten under the bench.
Built in the sixteenth century, the castle attracts thousands of visitors.
Having lost all his money in investments, he had to start over.
Not wanting to wake the baby, David crept silently into the kitchen.
examples.highlight: Not wanting to wake the baby

examples.en: Frightened by the loud thunder, the dog hid beneath the sofa.

mistakes.wrong: Walking into the room, the window was broken.
mistakes.right: Walking into the room, I noticed the window was broken.
mistakes.note: This creates a 'dangling participle' where the window appears to be walking into the room.

mistakes.wrong: Finished his dinner, he washed the dishes.
mistakes.right: Having finished his dinner, he washed the dishes.
mistakes.note: To show an active action completed prior to another, use the perfect participle 'Having finished'.

mistakes.wrong: Not have seen the film, I cannot comment on it.
mistakes.right: Not having seen the film, I cannot comment on it.
mistakes.note: Participle clauses must use the participle form (-ing), so use 'Not having seen'.

quiz.question: ___ all day in the hot sun, the gardeners were eager for a cold drink.
quiz.explanation: 'Having worked' highlights that working all day happened prior to their eagerness for a drink.

quiz.question: ___ by his friends, Liam decided to enter the singing competition.
quiz.explanation: Liam received the encouragement (passive meaning), so the past participle 'Encouraged' is required.

quiz.question: Not ___ where the station was, we stopped to ask a police officer.
quiz.explanation: Use the negative present participle 'Not knowing' to state the reason why we stopped.

quiz.question: The laptop ___ on the kitchen counter belongs to my roommate.
quiz.explanation: This acts as a reduced relative clause: 'The laptop (which is) charging on the counter'.

tip: Always check that the subject of the main clause matches the implied subject of your participle clause to avoid confusing dangling participles.

title: -ed vs -ing Adjectives
subtitle: Distinguishing feelings from characteristics
keyPoint: Use -ed adjectives to describe how someone feels, and use -ing adjectives to describe the person, thing, or situation causing that feeling.

cells: Describes a temporary state or feeling (the receiver)
The audience was captivated by the speech.
Describes the quality or cause of the feeling (the trigger)
The speaker gave an inspiring presentation.
bored = feeling tired of something; boring = uninteresting
He was bored because the lecture was boring.
confused = puzzled; confusing = hard to understand
The instructions are confusing, so I am confused.

useCases.label: Emotional States (-ed)
useCases.example: She felt completely overwhelmed by the amount of work.

useCases.label: Sources of Emotion (-ing)
useCases.example: Climbing Mount Everest must be a terrifying challenge.

useCases.label: Comparing Both in One Context
useCases.example: I was disappointed because the movie's ending was disappointing.

examples.en: Are you interested in joining our community sports club?
That mystery novel had a very surprising plot twist at the end.
We were utterly exhausted after hiking up the steep mountain all afternoon.
Listening to him talk about taxes for three hours was deeply boring.
Many people find public speaking to be an intimidating experience.

mistakes.wrong: I am so boring in this class.
mistakes.right: I am so bored in this class.
mistakes.note: 'I am boring' means you are an uninteresting person; 'I am bored' means you feel lack of interest.

mistakes.wrong: The documentary was very fascinated.
mistakes.right: The documentary was very fascinating.
mistakes.note: The documentary causes the interest, so it takes the active -ing participle adjective.

mistakes.wrong: Her explanation made me feel confusing.
mistakes.right: Her explanation made me feel confused.
mistakes.note: You experience the mental confusion, so use the -ed form ('confused').

quiz.question: The long flight from Tokyo to London was extremely ___.
quiz.explanation: The flight is the thing that causes fatigue, so the -ing adjective 'tiring' is required.

quiz.question: He was pleasantly ___ to find that his lost luggage had been returned.
quiz.explanation: He experienced the feeling of surprise, so use the -ed adjective 'surprised'.

quiz.question: Her remarks were rather ___ and left many attendees upset.
quiz.explanation: The remarks caused offense to others, so the active -ing form 'insulting' is correct.

quiz.question: The children were so ___ on Christmas morning that they woke up at five.
quiz.explanation: The children felt the emotion of excitement, requiring the -ed adjective 'excited'.

tip: Think of '-ed' as meaning 'affected by an emotion' and '-ing' as meaning 'producing that emotion'.

title: Concession Linkers
subtitle: Connecting contrasting facts with although, despite, and whereas
keyPoint: Use conjunctions like 'although' before a full clause (subject + verb), but use prepositions like 'despite' before nouns or gerunds (-ing).

cells: Although it rained heavily, we enjoyed the hike.
Despite the heavy rain, we enjoyed the hike.
Despite the fact that it rained, we enjoyed the hike.
Carl loves spicy food, whereas his sister dislikes it.

useCases.label: Direct Concession (Clauses)
useCases.example: Even though he had very little experience, he got the job.

useCases.label: Concession with Nouns
useCases.example: In spite of her nervousness, she delivered an exceptional speech.

useCases.label: Balanced Contrast
useCases.example: The north of the country is industrial, whereas the south relies on agriculture.

examples.en: Although they set out late, they managed to catch the last ferry.
In spite of working overtime all week, he missed the deadline.
Despite his considerable wealth, he lived in a remarkably modest house.
Some people thrive under pressure, whereas others find it debilitating.
Even though she had revised thoroughly, the final exam felt challenging.

mistakes.wrong: Despite he was ill, he attended the meeting.
mistakes.right: Although he was ill, he attended the meeting.
mistakes.note: 'Despite' cannot be followed directly by a subject and finite verb; use 'although' or 'despite being ill'.

mistakes.wrong: In spite of the rain was heavy, we went out.
mistakes.right: In spite of the heavy rain, we went out.
mistakes.note: 'In spite of' is a prepositional phrase and must take a noun phrase or gerund, not a full clause.

mistakes.wrong: Despite of the high prices, the cafe was crowded.
mistakes.right: Despite the high prices, the cafe was crowded.
mistakes.note: Never add 'of' after 'despite'. Only write 'in spite of' or 'despite'.

quiz.question: ___ the fierce cold, thousands of runners completed the marathon.
quiz.explanation: 'The fierce cold' is a noun phrase, so the preposition 'Despite' is required.

quiz.question: ___ my father prefers living in the countryside, my mother loves big cities.
quiz.explanation: 'Whereas' shows a balanced contrast between two independent clauses.

quiz.question: We had a fantastic time on vacation ___ the hotel room was tiny.
quiz.explanation: 'Even though' connects to the full clause 'the hotel room was tiny'.

quiz.question: She accepted the promotion, in spite ___ knowing it would mean longer hours.
quiz.explanation: The fixed prepositional phrase is always 'in spite of'.

tip: Remember: 'in spite OF' has three words, but 'DESPITE' is a single word and NEVER takes 'of'.

title: Future in the Past
subtitle: Talking about plans, intentions, and predictions made in the past
keyPoint: Express future plans viewed from a past perspective using 'was/were going to' for unfulfilled intentions or 'would' for past predictions.

cells: Intention or plan that usually did not happen
I was going to call you, but my battery died.
Past prediction or reported future of 'will'
She knew that the journey would be dangerous.
He was later to become Prime Minister.
Action that was imminent in the past
We were about to leave when the phone rang.

useCases.label: Unfulfilled Past Plans
useCases.example: They were going to fly to Rome, but their flight got canceled.

useCases.label: Past Predictions & Promises
useCases.example: He promised that he would arrive before midnight.

useCases.label: Interrupted Immediate Actions
useCases.example: I was about to pay the bill when I realized my wallet was gone.

examples.en: I was going to invite him, but I completely forgot.
Little did the explorers know that this decision would change history.
She was about to step onto the train when someone shouted her name.
We were going to buy the tickets online, but the website crashed.
They had a strong hunch that the business venture would succeed.

mistakes.wrong: I was to go to call you last night.
mistakes.right: I was going to call you last night.
mistakes.note: Use 'was going to + base verb' to describe an intended action in the past.

mistakes.wrong: He told me yesterday that he will help me today.
mistakes.right: He told me yesterday that he would help me today.
mistakes.note: Backshift 'will' to 'would' when reporting a promise or statement from a past perspective.

mistakes.wrong: I was about to leaving the house when it started raining.
mistakes.right: I was about to leave the house when it started raining.
mistakes.note: 'About to' is followed by a bare infinitive, not an -ing participle.

quiz.question: We ___ eat dinner at that Italian bistro, but it was fully booked.
quiz.explanation: 'Were going to' expresses an intention formed in the past that ultimately did not happen.

quiz.question: Back in 2010, nobody could imagine how popular smartphones ___ become.
quiz.explanation: 'Would' represents the past perspective of a future prediction (the past of 'will').

quiz.question: Quiet! The concert was just ___ begin when the power went out.
quiz.explanation: 'Was about to' indicates an event on the verge of happening in the past.

quiz.question: Sandra assured everyone that she ___ complete the proposal on time.
quiz.explanation: In indirect speech anchored in the past ('assured'), future 'will' changes to 'would'.

tip: Use 'was/were going to' when you want to give an excuse for something you intended to do but never actually finished.
